docs.title: Apitomy Axiom
docs.text: A workflow-first, event-driven orchestration platform that monitors GitHub and Jira activity and runs versioned workflows that delegate work to AI agents, scripts, and humans.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Workflows — visually authored, versioned automations with action, human-task, wait, and receive-event nodes; workflow runs are the primary object in the UI
  • Standard Workflow Inputs — a workflow's Start node declares the standard inputs it needs (subject, event), and Axiom supplies them when a run starts
  • Event Sources & Subscriptions — polls GitHub and Jira for activity, then routes matched events to workflows: create-workflow starts a run, workflow-dispatch resumes waiting runs
  • Schedule Triggers — cron schedules that start workflow runs on a fixed subject
  • Workflow Workbench — an authoring workspace for a workflow and its action types, tools and subscriptions, with a workflow canvas, editors, test runs, run history and an AI Assistant that proposes changes you can review or apply live
  • Subjects — the issue, pull request, or named subject a run is about, with a shared workspace and thread
  • Human + AI Agents — pluggable agent pool supports Claude Code, OpenCode, GitHub Copilot CLI, and human-completed tasks
  • Inbox & Dashboards — human tasks waiting for a person, and configurable dashboards
  • Web UI — React + PatternFly UI with real-time SSE updates
  • AI Assistant — interactive conversational interface with customizable session templates, real-time tool permission management, and plan mode
  • Pluggable AI Agents — swap between Claude Code CLI, OpenCode, and GitHub Copilot CLI without code changes

docs.title: Community
docs.text:
All Apitomy projects are open source under the Apache License 2.0. We welcome contributions, feedback, and ideas.

  • Issues: Report bugs and request features on GitHub Issues
  • Contributing: See the Contributing Guide

docs.title: API-First Development
docs.text: Axiom follows a contract-first API design. The OpenAPI specification is the source of truth — JAX-RS interfaces are generated from it at build time, and backend resource classes implement those generated interfaces.

docs.title: The OpenAPI Contract
docs.text:
The API specification lives at:

common/api/src/main/resources/openapi.json

All REST endpoints, request/response schemas, and path parameters are defined here. This file is the starting point for any API change.

docs.title: Code Generation
docs.text:
The common/api module uses the Apitomy Codegen Maven plugin to generate JAX-RS interfaces from the OpenAPI spec at compile time.

Generated output goes to:

common/api/target/generated-sources/jaxrs/io/apitomy/axiom/api/

The generated code includes:

  • Resource interfaces — one per API tag/group, with JAX-RS annotations (@Path, @GET, @POST, etc.)
  • Bean classes (package io.apitomy.axiom.api.beans) — POJOs with Jackson @JsonProperty annotations for request/response bodies

Resource methods take and return these generated beans. Do not use raw JsonNode for request or response bodies.

The plugin is configured in common/api/pom.xml:

<plugin>
    <groupId>io.apitomy</groupId>
    <artifactId>apitomy-codegen-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <projectSettings>
            <javaPackage>io.apitomy.axiom.api</javaPackage>
            <generatesOpenApi>false</generatesOpenApi>
        </projectSettings>
        <inputSpec>${project.basedir}/src/main/resources/openapi.json</inputSpec>
    </configuration>
</plugin>

docs.title: Implementing Endpoints
docs.text:
Backend implementations live in:

app/src/main/java/io/apitomy/axiom/app/rest/

Each resource class implements the corresponding generated interface:

@ApplicationScoped
public class SubjectsResourceImpl implements SubjectsResource {

    @Override
    public SubjectSearchResults listSubjects(/* params */) {
        // implementation
    }
}

The generated interface provides the JAX-RS annotations — the implementation class only needs to provide the business logic. Never put @Path on an implementation class; the paths come from the generated interface.

docs.title: Step 1: Edit the OpenAPI Spec
docs.text: Add the path, operation, and any new schemas to common/api/src/main/resources/openapi.json.

docs.title: Step 2: Regenerate Interfaces
docs.text:
mvn -q -pl common/api install

This regenerates the JAX-RS interfaces and beans and installs the module, so that app builds against the new interface (./build.sh also does this). Check target/generated-sources/jaxrs/io/apitomy/axiom/api/ to see the new interface method.

docs.title: Step 3: Implement the Endpoint
docs.text: In app/src/main/java/io/apitomy/axiom/app/rest/, either update an existing *ResourceImpl.java or create a new one implementing the generated interface.

docs.title: Step 4: Add UI API Functions
docs.text:
In ui/src/config/api.ts (or ui/src/config/compositions.ts for the workbench /compositions API), add:

  1. TypeScript interfaces matching the request/response schemas
  2. A fetch() function calling the new endpoint

Most API functions in api.ts follow the same pattern:

const API = `${getApiBaseUrl()}/api/v1`;

export async function fetchWidgets(): Promise<Widget[]> {
    const resp = await fetch(`${API}/widgets`);
    if (!resp.ok) throw new Error(await extractErrorMessage(resp, "Failed to fetch widgets"));
    return resp.json();
}

docs.title: API Base URL
docs.text:
The API base URL is resolved differently in development and production:

Mode Base URL Mechanism Development (empty string) Vite proxy forwards /api to the backend (localhost:9090 by default) Production (empty string) The backend serves the UI and the API from the same origin

This is handled by getApiBaseUrl() in api.ts. If a global window.AXIOM_API_URL string is defined, it is used as the base URL instead; the backend does not set it.

docs.title: SPA Routing
docs.text:
SpaRoutingFilter.java in the app module catches all non-API routes and forwards them to index.html, allowing React Router to handle client-side navigation.

Routes that are not forwarded:

  • /api/* — REST API endpoints
  • /q/* — Quarkus dev UI and health endpoints
  • Paths with file extensions (e.g. .js, .css, .png)

Everything else returns index.html, and React Router renders the correct page based on the URL.

docs.title: Building Axiom
docs.text: This guide covers how to build, run, and develop Axiom locally.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Requirement Purpose Java 25+ Backend compilation and runtime Maven 3.9+ Build system Node.js 20.19+ or 22.12+ and npm UI build (auto-installed by Maven in release builds) and runtime support for custom MCP tool servers and the AI Assistant's MCP server AI agent CLI One of claude, opencode, or copilot for AI features API key ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or provider-specific key

docs.title: Build Scripts
docs.text: Axiom provides several shell scripts in the project root for common workflows.

docs.title: build.sh — Standard Build
docs.text:
Builds the backend and runs unit tests. Does not build the UI.

./build.sh

Runs: mvn clean package. Extra arguments are passed to Maven, so ./build.sh -Pui also builds the UI and runs the UI unit tests (see below).

docs.title: UI Tests
docs.text:
The UI has unit and component tests written with Vitest and Testing Library. Run them on their own with:

cd ui && npm test

They also run as part of any Maven build with the -Pui profile (./build.sh -Pui, ./build-release.sh), so a failing UI test fails the build.

docs.title: build-release.sh — Release Build
docs.text:
Builds the complete application with the React UI bundled into a single runnable JAR.

./build-release.sh

Runs: mvn clean package -Pui,prod

The -Pui profile activates the ui-bundle module, which uses the frontend-maven-plugin to install Node.js, run npm install, npm run build and npm test, and package the resulting dist/ folder into META-INF/resources/ inside the JAR.

The -Pprod profile configures Quarkus to produce an uber-jar.

Output: app/target/apitomy-axiom-app-<version>-runner.jar (the release workflow republishes this as apitomy-axiom-<version>.jar)

The resulting application can be started with:

java -jar app/target/apitomy-axiom-app-<version>-runner.jar

docs.title: build-all.sh — Full Build with Integration Tests
docs.text:
Intended for a full build including tests that need a real AI agent CLI. The script warns if the claude CLI is not on the PATH or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is not set.

./build-all.sh

Runs: mvn clean package, after checking for Java 25, Maven and the claude CLI. Extra arguments are passed to Maven.

Tests tagged live-cli start a real opencode or claude CLI and may consume tokens. They are excluded by default. Enable them with the live-cli-tests profile:

./build-all.sh -Plive-cli-tests

docs.title: dev.sh — Development Mode
docs.text:
Builds all Maven modules, then launches the packaged backend JAR together with the Vite UI dev server side by side.

./dev.sh
Service URL Backend http://localhost:9090 Frontend (Vite dev server) http://localhost:9191

The Vite dev server proxies /api requests to the backend, so you access the UI at http://localhost:9191 and API calls are forwarded automatically.

Both processes run in the foreground — Ctrl+C stops everything.

Note

dev.sh runs the backend as a packaged application (mvn clean install followed by java -jar), not Quarkus's live-reload dev mode. Backend Java changes require re-running dev.sh to take effect. To get Quarkus hot reload while iterating on backend code, run mvn quarkus:dev directly from the app module instead.

Flags:

Flag Effect --skip-ui Start backend only, no Vite dev server --persist Use file-based H2 database (survives restarts) --portOffset=N Offset both the backend and UI dev server ports by N --dataDir=PATH Store the H2 database in PATH (implies --persist) 
./dev.sh --skip-ui              # Backend only
./dev.sh --persist              # Persistent database
./dev.sh --persist --skip-ui    # Both flags
./dev.sh --portOffset=100       # Backend on 9190, UI on 9291
./dev.sh --dataDir=/tmp/axiom   # Persistent database in /tmp/axiom

docs.title: Maven Profiles
docs.text: Profile What it does Activated by ui Includes the ui-bundle module (builds and packages the React UI) -Pui prod Produces an uber-jar with production settings -Pprod or auto in build-release.sh live-cli-tests Runs tests tagged live-cli, which start a real agent CLI -Plive-cli-tests

docs.title: UI Build Pipeline
docs.text:
When the ui profile is active, the ui-bundle module runs these steps:

  1. Install Node.js — frontend-maven-plugin downloads Node.js to ui-bundle/target/node-install/
  2. Install dependencies — runs npm install in the ui/ directory
  3. Build UI — runs npm run build, producing optimized assets in ui/dist/
  4. Package — copies ui/dist/ to target/classes/META-INF/resources/, where Quarkus serves them as static files

In production, the backend serves the bundled UI directly — no separate web server needed.

docs.title: Development Workflow
docs.text:
A typical development loop:

  1. Run ./dev.sh to start both backend and frontend
  2. Open http://localhost:9191 in your browser
  3. Edit frontend TypeScript/React code — Vite hot-reloads instantly
  4. Edit backend Java code — re-run ./dev.sh (or use mvn quarkus:dev from the app module for hot reload)

  5. Run the tests of one module (and build the modules it depends on) from the project root, for example:

    mvn -q -pl app -am test -Dtest=WorkflowScheduleTriggersResourceTest

    Add -Dsurefire.failIfNoSpecifiedTests=false when the selected test class is not present in every built module.

docs.title: Port Reference
docs.text: Port Service Mode 9090 Backend Development (./dev.sh or mvn quarkus:dev) 9191 Vite UI dev server Development (./dev.sh or npm run dev) 9191 Backend Production (release JAR)

docs.title: Database Profiles
docs.text:
Profile Database Schema Management dev (default) H2 in-memory Hibernate drop-and-create — recreated on restart persist H2 file (<axiom.home>/data/axiom, default ~/.axiom/data/axiom) Flyway migrations prod H2 file (<axiom.home>/data/axiom, default ~/.axiom/data/axiom) Flyway migrations

Use --persist with dev.sh or -Dquarkus.profile=persist with Maven to keep data between restarts during development.

See the Database & Migrations guide for details on schema management, and Upgrading and Backups for what to back up alongside the database.

docs.title: Correlation by Trace ID
docs.text: Axiom uses the trace ID as its correlation ID. Every unit of work — a workflow run and the tasks its nodes create — is identified by its trace ID. Every record produced by that work stores the trace ID, so given one trace ID you can find everything that belongs to that unit of work. See Tracing for the trace model itself.

docs.title: Tables That Carry trace_id
docs.text:
Table Notes task Trace the task runs in workflow_run Trace of the workflow run routing_outcome Trace of the run the routing rule started activity_log Trace of the work that wrote the row ai_usage Trace of the work that incurred the cost

All columns are nullable UUIDs with no foreign key. Trace data has a bounded lifetime: when TraceCleanup deletes a trace, it clears trace_id on activity_log, ai_usage, task, workflow_run and routing_outcome. It also clears trace_node_id on routing_outcome_item and workflow_run_resume for the deleted trace's nodes. See Data Retention.

docs.title: Finding All Records for a Trace
docs.text:
• GET /traces/{id} returns the trace tree (nodes, tool calls).
  • GET /activity?filterTraceId={id} returns the activity rows for the trace.
  • GET /usage/ai?filterTraceId={id} returns the AI usage rows for the trace.
  • Tasks and workflow runs expose a traceId field.

For both filters, a malformed filterTraceId returns 400 Bad Request.

In the UI, the Activity log and AI usage pages show a Trace column that links to /logs/traces/:traceId, and a Trace ID filter. Both pages accept a ?traceId= query parameter as a deep link, for example /logs/activity?traceId=....

docs.title: Agent Calls: Joining the Caller's Trace
docs.text:
When an agent calls Axiom APIs through the Axiom MCP server, sdk-server.js sends two headers on every request when the matching environment variables are set:

Header Source variable X-Axiom-Trace-Id AXIOM_TRACE_ID X-Axiom-Parent-Node-Id AXIOM_PARENT_NODE_ID

CallerTraceFilter validates the headers in this order:

  1. The trace ID is a valid UUID.
  2. The trace exists.
  3. The trace status is in-progress.
  4. The parent node belongs to that trace. If the parent node header is missing, the trace's root node is used.

If any check fails, the headers are removed and ignored, and a debug log is written. A request never fails because of these headers.

A valid caller trace is put into the logging MDC for the rest of the request, so server log lines written while handling the agent's call carry the caller's trace ID. No endpoint creates work in the caller's trace: tasks are created only by workflow nodes, in the run's own trace.

docs.title: Server Logs: Correlation IDs in the MDC
docs.text:
Server log lines carry the correlation IDs of the work they belong to. The IDs are put into the logging MDC (org.jboss.logging.MDC) by io.apitomy.axiom.core.logging.LogContext:

MDC key Value traceId Trace (correlation) ID eventId Stream event being routed subjectId Subject taskId Task workflowRunId Workflow run

LogContext also maintains the composite key axiomCtx, which holds only the keys that are present, for example [traceId=3f2a9c1e-... subjectId=7 taskId=42], and is absent when none are set. The console and file log formats in application.properties print it with %X{axiomCtx}, so lines outside any unit of work look exactly as before:

2026-10-03 11:53:27 INFO  [io.ap.ax.ap.TaskExecutionService] (main) [traceId=3f2a9c1e-... subjectId=7 taskId=42] Task 42 completed
2026-10-03 11:53:27 INFO  [io.ap.ax.ap.EventStreamOrchestrator] (executor-thread-1) Recovered 2 orphaned pending ledger entries

docs.title: Grepping the Logs
docs.text:
Given a trace ID (from the trace UI, a task, a workflow run or a routing_outcome row):

grep 'traceId=3f2a9c1e-0000-4000-8000-000000000001' axiom.log
# Everything for one task, workflow run or stream event
grep -E 'taskId=42[] ]' axiom.log
grep -E 'workflowRunId=17[] ]' axiom.log
grep 'eventId=6b1d...' axiom.log

Match numeric IDs with a trailing ] or space (as above) so that taskId=4 does not also match taskId=42. The console log goes to standard output; the file log is written only when quarkus.log.file.enabled=true.

A failed routing rule logs two lines: Routing rule <type> failed for event <id>: <message>, written inside the rule's context (so it carries the eventId and the rule's traceId) and without a stack trace, and then Routing failed for event <id> / subscription <id>, written in the event's context (eventId only) with the stack trace. The stack trace is logged once, on the second line, because not every routing failure passes through a rule. To find the stack trace for a trace ID, grep the trace ID, then grep the eventId shown on the rule line.

docs.title: Where the Context Is Set
docs.text: Entry point Keys EventStreamOrchestrator, per event and ledger retry eventId; per routing rule also traceId once the started run's trace exists TaskExecutionService.executeTask, onTaskCompleted, failTask traceId, eventId, subjectId, taskId, workflowRunId ScriptExecutionService.executeScript (incl. the async script body) as for tasks WorkflowExecutionService start and advance (task completion, wait elapsed, event received) traceId, subjectId, workflowRunId CallerTraceFilter (REST requests with a valid X-Axiom-Trace-Id) traceId

docs.title: Rules for New Code
docs.text:
• Always use try-with-resources: try (LogContext ignored = LogContext.create().traceId(id).taskId(t)) {...}. close() restores the previous values, so contexts nest (a task started during event routing logs with the task's trace, then the event's context is back) and nothing leaks to the next job on a pooled, virtual or scheduler thread, including when the body throws.
  • The MDC belongs to the current thread (or, on Vert.x, to the request's duplicated context). Work handed to another thread loses it. Agent completion callbacks (CompletableFuture.thenAccept / exceptionally) run on the agent's thread, usually a common ForkJoinPool worker, so they are wrapped with LogContext.wrap(...), which captures the context when the callback is created and restores it, and removes it again, around the callback. Do the same for new asynchronous code, or open a LogContext inside the asynchronous body as ScriptExecutionService does.
  • Code running inside agent subprocess readers (agents/*) runs on threads Axiom does not wrap; those lines have no correlation IDs.

docs.title: OpenTelemetry (Follow-Up Evaluation)
docs.text:
quarkus-opentelemetry would add W3C trace context propagation, spans for REST, JDBC and the scheduler, and export to a collector (Jaeger, Tempo). With it enabled, Quarkus also puts its own traceId/spanId in the MDC. Notes for a follow-up:

  • OpenTelemetry trace IDs are 32 hex characters; Axiom trace IDs are UUIDs stored in the database. They would be separate IDs. Keep the Axiom trace ID as the correlation ID and add it as a span attribute (axiom.trace_id) rather than trying to make the two equal. The MDC key traceId would clash with the OpenTelemetry one; rename ours (for example axiomTraceId) at that point.
  • Context propagation across the CompletableFuture callbacks and scheduler threads has the same problem as the MDC and would need the same wrapping (or SmallRye Context Propagation's ManagedExecutor).
  • It needs a collector to be useful; Axiom is a single-process app with its own trace UI, so the benefit is mainly for deployments that already run an observability stack. It is not added for now.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• Any in-progress trace can be named in the caller headers. There is no check that the caller belongs to the same subject; the header only affects log correlation.
  • Assistant sessions (AssistantSessionManager) are not traced. Their AI usage rows have no trace ID.
  • Script-mode tasks have no ai_usage row, because no AI is invoked.
  • The lineage view that follows these links across entities is described in Lineage.

docs.title: Data Retention
docs.text:
Axiom deletes old data with scheduled cleanup jobs in app/src/main/java/io/apitomy/axiom/app/. The retention periods live in the single-row retention_config table and are edited on the Data Retention page (/data-retention) or with GET/PUT /api/v1/system/retention.

The rule for every cleanup job is: after it runs, no row points at a deleted row, except for the documented soft references listed under Accepted dangling references.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Column API field Default Cleanup job inactive_subject_retention_days inactiveSubjectRetentionDays 90 InactiveSubjectCleanup trace_retention_days traceRetentionDays 30 TraceCleanup event_retention_days eventRetentionDays 90 StreamEventCleanup workflow_run_retention_days workflowRunRetentionDays 0 HistoryCleanup activity_log_retention_days activityLogRetentionDays 0 HistoryCleanup ai_usage_retention_days aiUsageRetentionDays 0 HistoryCleanup

For the three history settings, 0 means keep forever, and 0 is the default. Negative values are rejected with 400. The inactive-subject, trace and event settings must be at least 1, because 0 would delete everything; smaller values are also rejected with 400. A PUT that omits any setting (or sends null) leaves its current value unchanged.

docs.title: Batching and Retries
docs.text:
Every job runs hourly. TraceCleanup, StreamEventCleanup and HistoryCleanup are batched: they are staggered with delayed start times of 3, 6 and 9 minutes, select at most 500 IDs (BATCH_SIZE) per transaction, and delete by those IDs or with sub-selects, never with an unbounded IN list. Each batch runs in its own transaction through CleanupRetry, which retries database lock failures. Each of these three jobs has a package-private doCleanup() that runs all batches in the caller's transaction; tests use it.

InactiveSubjectCleanup is not batched. It runs hourly without a start delay and deletes all qualifying subjects in one @Transactional method through SubjectDeletionService, without CleanupRetry.

docs.title: TraceCleanup
docs.text:
Deletes traces whose started_on is older than the retention period, with their trace_node and tool_execution rows. Before deleting, it clears (sets to NULL):

  • trace_id on task, workflow_run, routing_outcome, activity_log and ai_usage;
  • trace_node_id on routing_outcome_item and workflow_run_resume, for the deleted trace's nodes.

TraceCleanupTest.everyTraceColumnIsHandled scans every entity for columns named trace_id, *_trace_id or trace_node_id and fails if one is not in its list of handled columns. When you add such a column, clear it in TraceCleanup, add it to the assertions in TraceCleanupTest, and add it to the list.

docs.title: StreamEventCleanup
docs.text:
Deletes stream events older than the retention period, with their ledger entries, routing outcomes and routing outcome items. An event is kept while a workflow run with status running or waiting:

  • has it as trigger_event_id, or
  • has a workflow_run_resume row with that event_id.

Such an event becomes eligible on the first cleanup after the run finishes, so the run → event link is never lost while the run can still use it. The job also deletes event source poll logs older than 3 days.

docs.title: InactiveSubjectCleanup / SubjectDeletionService
docs.text:
Deletes inactive subjects — subjects with no running or waiting workflow run — whose most recent run finished (completed_on) longer ago than the retention period. Subjects that have never had a run are not deleted automatically. The same SubjectDeletionService code runs when a subject is deleted through the API. It deletes the subject's thread entries, AI usage, activity log entries, tasks, workflow runs and their waits, event subscriptions and resume rows, and its workspace directory (subject-<id>).

Traces and routing outcomes are event history, not subject data, so they are kept and their references are cleared: trace.subject_id, routing_outcome.subject_id and task_id, and routing_outcome_item subject_id, task_id and workflow_run_id.

docs.title: HistoryCleanup
docs.text:
Each setting is skipped when it is 0.

Data Deleted rows Workflow runs Status completed, failed or cancelled, and completed_on (or started_on if unset) older than the period Activity log created_on older than the period, with or without a subject AI usage created_on older than the period, with or without a subject

Workflow runs use an allow-list of finished statuses (FINISHED_WORKFLOW_RUN_STATUSES), so runs in a status added later are kept until the list is updated. Deleting a workflow run deletes its workflow_wait, workflow_event_subscription and workflow_run_resume rows and clears task.workflow_run_id and routing_outcome_item.workflow_run_id. Tasks are kept: they belong to the subject and are deleted with it. The run's trace follows trace retention.

docs.title: Data Not Covered by Retention
docs.text: Workbench test runs of draft action types and tools (CompositionTestRuns) are not stored in the database. They are kept in memory, at most 50 per composition (the oldest is dropped first), and are lost when the server restarts. Deleting a composition drops its test runs. They create no traces, tasks or workflow runs, so no cleanup job handles them.

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text: The cleanup jobs use bulk JPQL UPDATE and DELETE statements, which bypass the persistence context. If another transaction has the same row loaded as a managed entity (for example a task whose trace_id is being cleared) and flushes it after the cleanup commits, it can write the old value back, or fail on a row that no longer exists. The window is small, because cleanup only touches rows that are past their retention period, and this was already true before #429. The next cleanup run clears any value that was written back.

docs.title: Accepted Dangling References
docs.text:
These columns are soft references with no foreign key. They are kept on purpose so history survives, and consumers must treat them as possibly dangling:

  • event_id on trace, task, activity_log, ai_usage and workflow_run_resume, ledger_id on workflow_run_resume, and trigger_event_id / trigger_ledger_id on workflow_run, after event retention deletes the event of a finished run (see Tracing and Event System Design).
  • trace_node.entity_type / entity_id, which are free-form display references.

docs.title: Database & Migrations
docs.text: Axiom uses H2 as its database with Hibernate Panache for ORM and Flyway for schema migrations.

docs.title: Database Profiles
docs.text:
Axiom has three database configurations, selected via Quarkus profiles:

Profile Storage Schema Management Use Case dev (default) H2 in-memory Hibernate drop-and-create Fast development — schema rebuilt on every restart persist H2 file (<axiom.home>/data/axiom, default ~/.axiom/data/axiom) Flyway migrations Development with persistent data prod H2 file (<axiom.home>/data/axiom, default ~/.axiom/data/axiom) Flyway migrations Production (uber-jar)

Activate the persist profile during development:

./dev.sh --persist
# or, with the database in another directory
./dev.sh --dataDir=/path/to/data
# or
mvn quarkus:dev -Dquarkus.profile=persist

The prod profile is activated automatically when running from the release JAR.

docs.title: Entity Model
docs.text: All entities are in core/src/main/java/io/apitomy/axiom/core/entities/ and extend Quarkus PanacheEntity (or PanacheEntityBase for entities with non-Long primary keys, such as TraceEntity's UUID key), which provides the active record pattern. Read the entity classes directly for the current field list — that is the authoritative reference, not this guide.

docs.title: Active Record Pattern
docs.text:
Entities use the Panache active record style — queries are static methods on the entity class:

// Find by ID
SubjectEntity subject = SubjectEntity.findById(id);

// Query with parameters
List<TaskEntity> tasks = TaskEntity.find("subjectId = ?1 and status = ?2",
    subjectId, "Pending").list();

// Persist
entity.persist();

// Count
long count = StreamEventEntity.count("source", "github");

No separate DAO or repository classes are needed.

docs.title: Flyway Migrations
docs.text:
Schema migrations live in:

app/src/main/resources/db/migration/

Flyway runs automatically at startup when the persist or prod profile is active.

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text:
Axiom 3 starts from a single baseline migration:

app/src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__baseline.sql

V1__baseline.sql is frozen as of 3.0.0. Never edit it. Every schema change is a new, incremental migration, V2__<description>.sql, V3__<description>.sql and so on, which Flyway applies at startup to existing databases. A migration must work against real data written by the previous release, and must keep working on the H2 file database used by the persist and prod profiles.

docs.title: Databases From Earlier Major Versions
docs.text: Axiom 3 cannot use a database created by Axiom 2.x or older. LegacyDatabaseGuard (a Flyway callback that runs before validation) refuses to start with a clear message when the database's migration history contains anything other than Axiom 3's migrations (a version 2 or later from 2.x, or a Flyway baseline marker), or when the database has tables but no migration history. Flyway baselining (baseline-on-migrate) is therefore disabled. See Upgrading and Backups.

docs.title: Adding a New Entity
docs.text:
1. Create the entity class in core/src/main/java/io/apitomy/axiom/core/entities/:

    @Entity
@Table(name = "my_entity")
public class MyEntity extends PanacheEntity {
    @Column(nullable = false)
    public String name;

    @Column
    public String description;

    @Column(name = "created_on", nullable = false)
    public Instant createdOn;
}

  2. Add the table and its sequence to V1__baseline.sql:

    CREATE TABLE my_entity (
    id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    description VARCHAR(1024),
    created_on TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (id)
);
CREATE SEQUENCE my_entity_SEQ START WITH 1 INCREMENT BY 50;

    One sequence per entity. Every PanacheEntity gets its id from a sequence named <table>_SEQ with INCREMENT BY 50 (the Hibernate/Panache default allocationSize). The baseline must create that sequence. Forgetting this is invisible in tests, which use drop-and-create, but makes prod fail Hibernate validation with missing sequence.

  3. If the entity is API-exposed, update the OpenAPI spec and create/update the corresponding REST resource (see API-First Development).

docs.title: Adding a Column to an Existing Entity
docs.text:
1. Add the field to the entity class:

    @Column
public String priority;

  2. Add the column to the table's CREATE TABLE statement in V1__baseline.sql.

docs.title: Migration Guard Test
docs.text:
Tests run with Hibernate drop-and-create, so they never exercise the migrations. To catch drift between the migrations and the entity model, MigrationSchemaValidationTest (in app/src/test/java/io/apitomy/axiom/app/db/) runs in CI as a plain JUnit test (no Quarkus boot, a few seconds):

  1. Once per run, it applies the baseline to a fresh, private in-memory H2 database with Flyway's Java API.
  2. It builds Hibernate metadata from every @Entity in the core module's Jandex index and starts a session factory with hbm2ddl.auto=validate, which checks tables, columns, column types and sequences.
  3. It lists every sequence the entity model expects and reports all that are missing at once.

The guard covers H2 only; nothing in CI runs the migrations against PostgreSQL.

If you add or change an entity without updating V1__baseline.sql, this test fails. Fix the baseline; don't change the test.

docs.title: Development Tips
docs.text:
• In dev mode (default), Hibernate recreates the schema on every restart. You don't need Flyway migrations during development — just modify the entity class.
  • Switch to persist mode (--persist) when you want to test the baseline or keep data between restarts. After changing V1__baseline.sql, delete the persistent database first.
  • The H2 console is available at http://localhost:9090/q/h2 during development (Quarkus dev mode only).

See Upgrading and Backups for what a production upgrade can change and what needs to be backed up alongside the database.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Axiom's event system provides a three-layer architecture for monitoring external systems and reacting to changes:

  1. Event Sources — authenticated links to external systems (GitHub, Jira) that poll for changes and produce a normalized event stream
  2. Event Stream — a single database table of typed, schema-validated events from all event sources, browsable via REST API and UI
  3. Subscriptions — filtered views over the event stream with EL expression matching and configurable routing rules that send matched events to workflows (workflow creation and workflow dispatch)

docs.title: Event Sources (EventSourceEntity)
docs.text:
A configured, authenticated link to an external system. Produces a raw, normalized event stream. No filtering — every detectable event gets recorded.

  • Each event source has a user-provided slug ID as its primary key (lowercase letters, numbers, dashes; max 63 characters, e.g., github-com, github-ibm, jira-prod)
  • Multiple event sources of the same type are supported (e.g., github.com + GitHub Enterprise)
  • Each event source specifies what to watch (repositories for GitHub, projects for Jira)
  • A background poller runs per event source, iterating over watched resources
  • Poll results are audited in the event_source_poll_log table with status, timing, events ingested, and error details (3-day retention)
  • The event source's baseUrl identifies the server (e.g., https://github.com); for GitHub the poller resolves the web and API URLs from it (see "Base URL resolution" below)

GitHub event source: - Uses the Repository Events API (GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/events) - ETag-based conditional polling for efficiency (304 when nothing changed) - Per-repo polling under a shared authentication token - PR event payloads are truncated by the API; the poller backfills via GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{number} - Configuration: baseUrl (e.g., https://github.com), secretName, repositories (list of owner/repo), pollInterval

Jira event source: - Uses JQL search with changelog expansion (expand=changelog) - Single query covers all configured projects via a project in ("A", "B") clause (keys are quoted) - Field-level change detection from changelog entries; every event carries the issue state as of that event - ADF-to-plain-text conversion for description and comment bodies - Configuration: baseUrl (e.g., https://myorg.atlassian.net; must start with http:// or https://, a trailing / is removed when saved), secretName, projects (list of project keys matching ^[A-Z][A-Z0-9_]+$), optional extraFields (list of Jira field names), pollInterval

Authentication: Three-tier fallback for both types: per-event-source secret (by name from the secrets store), default provider secret (GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN for GitHub, JIRA_API_TOKEN for Jira), environment variable.

docs.title: Event Stream
docs.text:
A single stream_event database table of normalized, schema-validated events produced by all event sources.

  • Each event has a UUID primary key and a well-defined typed payload determined by its event type (26 types across issue, PR, and repository events)
  • Deduplication via unique index on source_event_id
  • Configurable retention via the eventRetentionDays setting
  • Browsable via REST API (GET /stream/events) and the Event Stream UI page

docs.title: Subscriptions (EventSubscription)
docs.text:
A filtered view over the event stream with configurable routing. Each subscription has:

  • Filter Expression — a Jakarta EL expression that evaluates to boolean against the event map (e.g., event.type.startsWith('pr.') && event.eventSourceId == 'github-com'). Empty expression matches all events.
  • Routing Rules — a list of destinations for matched events (see Routing below)
  • Labels — free-form strings for categorization and downstream scoping
  • Enabled/Disabled — subscriptions must be explicitly enabled to process events

Filter expression evaluation uses the flow engine's ConditionEvaluator (Jakarta EL). The event is exposed as an event variable with fields: type, source, eventSourceId, ref, timestamp, actor.*, and payload.* (with full typed payload field access).

docs.title: Routing Rules
docs.text:
Each subscription defines zero or more routing rules. When an event matches the filter expression, each routing rule executes in order. There are exactly two routing types:

Destination Type Config Required What Happens create-workflow workflowDefinitionId (or workflowDefinitionName, resolved to the id on save) Finds or auto-creates a Subject from the event's ref URL, then starts a new workflow run of the specified definition on that subject, with subjectId, ref, and event in its context. If the subject already has an active (running or waiting) run of that definition, no run is started or queued: the outcome records a skipped workflow-run item. workflow-dispatch None Broadcasts the event to every workflow run parked at a receive-event node whose event type and EL expression match (flow engine matchesEvent). When the event's ref correlates to a subject, delivery is limited to waiting runs on that subject (all of them, across definitions); otherwise all waiting runs with a matching event type are offered the event.

A subscription with no routing rules matches events silently (useful for previewing matches before committing to a routing destination).

Event processing is driven by EventStreamOrchestrator, a scheduled job that runs every axiom.stream-pipeline.poll-interval (default 5s). Each tick evaluates new events against enabled subscriptions, records the result in the processing ledger (below), runs the routing rules of matching subscriptions, and then retries failed ledger entries that are due.

docs.title: Starting a run from an event
docs.text:
create-workflow rules start runs through EventStreamOrchestrator.startRunFromEvent. The same method is used for two runs that are not started by a subscription:

  • Manual runs from an event. The event detail page's "Run workflow…" action (POST /stream/events/{eventId}/runs) starts any published workflow for the event. Workflows started by create-workflow rules of subscriptions that matched the event are suggested first (GET /stream/events/{eventId}/workflow-suggestions). The run gets the label trigger:manual in addition to any labels in the request.
  • Re-runs. POST /workflow/runs/{runId}/rerun re-runs a failed run. When the failed run was started from an event that still exists, the re-run is started from that event.

startRunFromEvent finds or creates the subject from the event's ref, puts the event into the run's context as event, and starts the run in its own transaction with the event recorded as its trigger. The run, its trace and its event context are the same however the run was started. The difference is the ledger: only a subscription's create-workflow rule has a ledger entry. Manual runs and re-runs write no ledger entry and no routing outcome, so their trigger_ledger_id is null. If the subject already has an active run of the workflow, a manual run fails with HTTP 409 (a routing rule records a skipped item instead).

docs.title: Processing Ledger
docs.text:
The event_processing_ledger table provides durable, restart-safe event processing. Each (event_id, subscription_id) pair gets a ledger entry with one of four statuses:

Status Meaning Next Action pending An attempt is in progress Transitions to completed, failed, exhausted (or skipped when a retry re-evaluates the filter). On startup, orphaned pending entries are recovered to failed and due immediately (exhausted if it was the last attempt). completed All routing rules executed successfully Terminal. skipped Filter did not match Terminal. Prevents re-evaluation on future ticks. failed The last attempt failed Retried automatically once next_attempt_at has passed (exponential backoff). exhausted The last allowed attempt failed Terminal unless retried manually (one more attempt).

Key behaviors: - Restart-safe: No in-memory state. The ledger is the complete record. - Cutoff-scoped, not fully retroactive: Each subscription has a processEventsFrom timestamp, defaulted to the moment the subscription is created (it can be set to an earlier or later time explicitly, e.g. via the API). Only events whose timestamp is at or after that cutoff are ever evaluated against the subscription. Enabling a subscription does not retroactively evaluate events that occurred before its cutoff. - Retry: Each ledger entry tracks its attempts: attempt_count (the first try included), last_attempt_at and, while it is failed, next_attempt_at. A failed attempt sets next_attempt_at = now + min(retry-initial-delay * 2^(n-1), retry-max-delay) where n is the number of the attempt that failed (defaults 30s and 1h: 30s, 1m, 2m, ... capped at 1h). The retry pass selects only failed entries whose next_attempt_at has passed (index on (status, next_attempt_at)), and never an entry attempted since the tick started, so the first pass and the retry pass cannot both run an entry in one tick. A retry marks the entry pending, increments attempt_count and sets last_attempt_at before routing, in one conditional update (... where id = ? and status = 'failed'). If it changes no row, a manual retry or another node got the entry first and it is skipped, so two nodes can never start the same attempt. A retry that re-evaluates the filter (see below) and marks the entry skipped still counts as an attempt. When the attempt that reaches axiom.stream-pipeline.max-attempts (default 3) fails, the entry becomes exhausted (a distinct status rather than failed with a null next_attempt_at, so lists, filters and the UI can tell "will retry" from "gave up" by status alone), "(giving up after N attempts)" is appended to its error message and a WARN is logged once. - Manual retry: POST /stream/events/{eventId}/processing/{ledgerId}/retry (the retry button on the event detail page) makes a failed or exhausted entry failed and due immediately, with one conditional update (... where status in ('failed', 'exhausted')); it returns 409 for any other status, including an attempt in progress (pending), so it can never make a running attempt due again or roll back its attempt count. It does not reset attempt_count, so attempt numbers keep increasing and an exhausted entry gets exactly one more attempt: if it fails it is exhausted again. - Attempt history: Every routing_outcome records its attempt_number, so the outcomes of an entry group into attempts; the processing API returns them all with the entry's attempt fields and the configured maximum. - Configuration validation: startup fails with a message naming the property when max-attempts < 1, retry-initial-delay <= 0 or retry-max-delay < retry-initial-delay. Invalid values are rejected rather than clamped, so a misconfiguration is never silently replaced. - No replay on retry: A retry skips routing rules that already have a completed outcome for the ledger entry, so a later rule's failure does not re-create tasks or workflows, or re-dispatch the event. Outcomes do not store the rule's position, so the k-th rule of a routing type is matched to the k-th completed outcome of that type. Rules run in order and stop at the first failure, so this is exact while the subscription's rules are unchanged; editing the rules between attempts can skip or replay the wrong rule. - Processing failures count: A failure outside the routing rules (building the event context or evaluating the filter) is recorded as a failed outcome with routing type processing, so it counts toward the attempt cap. On the first pass such a failure happens before the ledger entry exists, so it creates a failed entry (attempt 1); the pair then leaves the unledgered NOT IN query and is only retried by the retry pass, with backoff and the cap. A retry of an entry without any routing-rule outcome re-evaluates the filter, since it may never have matched, and marks the entry skipped if it does not match. An unparseable payload is not a failure: it is routed with an empty payload map, on the first pass and on retries alike. - Dedup: Unique constraint on (event_id, subscription_id) prevents duplicate processing. - Startup recovery: Orphaned pending entries from a previous crash are bulk-updated to failed on the first tick, then retried normally.

docs.title: Routing outcomes and items
docs.text:
Each routing rule run records one routing_outcome row per attempt (routing type, status, summary, trace ID, error). Everything the rule produced is recorded as routing_outcome_item rows, children of the outcome deleted with it (ON DELETE CASCADE; StreamEventCleanup also deletes them explicitly):

Item type Written by Links workflow-run create-workflow rule (status skipped when the subject already had an active run of the definition) workflow_run_id (not set when skipped), subject_id workflow-resumed workflow-dispatch rule, one per run the event resumed workflow_run_id, subject_id, trace_node_id (the receive-event node) no-match workflow-dispatch rule that resumed no run —

Each item has a status (completed, failed, or skipped), a summary and, when failed, an error_message. A workflow-dispatch rule writes one workflow-resumed item per resumed run, or a single no-match item (outcome summary "No waiting workflow run matched the event") when nothing matched, so "nothing happened" is recorded explicitly. A run that matched but failed to resume gets a failed workflow-resumed item with the error; the outcome stays completed so the rule is not retried (a retry would re-dispatch the event to every run). The processing API adds the run's traceId to workflow-run and workflow-resumed items, so the event page links to the run and its trace.

The outcome's own subject_id and task_id columns hold only the first subject and task; readers should use the items.

docs.title: Links between events and workflow runs
docs.text:
Events and workflow runs are linked both ways. None of these links are foreign keys: event retention deletes events and ledger entries while runs are kept (but never while the run is still running or waiting).

  • Started runs. A run started from an event (by a create-workflow rule, manually from the event, or as a re-run of a run started from an event) stores trigger_event_id; the run's workflow trace has eventId set to the event; and the run's context has the event ID as event.id. Only runs started by a create-workflow rule also store trigger_ledger_id, and their outcome's trace_id is the run's trace. Runs started any other way (a schedule trigger, or a re-run of such a run) have null trigger fields. GET /workflow/runs?triggerEventId=<id> lists the runs started from an event; the event detail page shows them on its "Runs" tab.
  • Resumed runs (workflow-dispatch). WorkflowEventDispatcher.dispatchStreamEvent returns the runs it resumed (run, node, trace and receive-event trace node). The workflow_event_subscription row is deleted when it is consumed, so each resumption is recorded as a workflow_run_resume row (run, node, event, ledger entry, trace node; deleted with the run), and the receive-event trace node's summary gets "resumed by event ". The event map passed to the run (event in its context) includes the event ID as id.
  • API. WorkflowInstance and WorkflowRunSummary expose triggerEventId and triggerLedgerId; WorkflowInstance.resumedBy lists the resuming events. The workflow run page shows "Triggered by" and "Resumed by" links to /events/stream/:id.

    • Items never affect retries: the attempt cap and the skip-on-retry rule count routing_outcome rows by status and routing type, not items. Each attempt persists its own outcome together with its items, so the items of an attempt stay on that attempt's outcome and never appear on a later attempt's outcome.

docs.title: Retention
docs.text:
• Stream events and ledger entries: Cleaned up hourly based on eventRetentionDays setting (default 90 days), in batches of 500. Routing outcomes and ledger entries are deleted first (FK), then events. Events that a running or waiting workflow run was started by (trigger_event_id) or resumed by (workflow_run_resume.event_id) are kept until the run finishes. See Data Retention.
  • Event source poll logs: Cleaned up hourly with a 3-day fixed retention.

docs.title: Configuration Packs
docs.text: Event sources and subscriptions are included in the configuration pack export/import system, allowing portable sharing of event system configuration.

docs.title: Event schemas
docs.text:
Every event type has a JSON Schema (draft 2020-12). The schema files live under core/src/main/resources/schemas/events/:

  • envelope.json — the common envelope (see below).
  • defs.json — shared $defs (Timestamp, NullableTimestamp, Actor, Change, CommitAuthor, Commit, NormalizedLabel, NormalizedComment, NormalizedIssue, NormalizedPullRequest, NormalizedReview).
  • payloads/<type>.json — one payload schema per event type, e.g. payloads/issue.closed.json.

These files are hand-maintained and are the source of truth. The script tools/generate-event-payload-schemas.py was used only to bootstrap them; do not re-run it.

EventSchemaRegistry loads the files at startup and assembles one self-contained schema per event type (envelope + payload + all of defs.json copied in as local $defs). If the schemas cannot be loaded, startup fails. The assembled schemas are served by GET /api/v1/schemas/events (summary list of type and description) and GET /api/v1/schemas/events/{eventType} (the schema; 404 for an unknown type). The paths use /schemas/events rather than /event-schemas because the code generator groups paths by the first word before -, which would collide with /event-sources.

sourceData (the raw source payload) is not validated; the schemas allow any object there.

docs.title: Runtime validation
docs.text: EventStreamService validates each event against its schema before persisting it. An invalid event is still saved, with the validation messages stored in stream_event.validation_errors and exposed as validationErrors on StreamEvent. Each invalid event is logged as a warning, and the poll log message gets the suffix (N failed schema validation). If the validator itself throws, the exception is recorded as a validation error rather than dropping the event.

docs.title: Drift tests and adding an event type
docs.text:
EventSchemaDriftTest checks that the EventType enum, the payload records registered in @JsonSubTypes, and the payload schema files stay in sync. ValidatingGitHubNormalizer and ValidatingJiraNormalizer wrap the normalizers in tests and validate every event they produce against the schemas, so a normalizer change that breaks a schema fails the build.

To add a new event type:

  1. Add the value to the EventType enum.
  2. Add a payload record in core/src/main/java/io/apitomy/axiom/core/events/model/payloads/.
  3. Register the record in the @JsonSubTypes list in EventPayload.java.
  4. Add payloads/<type>.json under core/src/main/resources/schemas/events/.

docs.title: Identity and timestamps
docs.text: Source event IDs are unique per event source: the unique key is (eventSourceId, sourceEventId) (migration V4__event_schema_validation.sql). All timestamps are ISO-8601 UTC strings ending in Z.

docs.title: Common Event Envelope
docs.text:
Every event in the stream shares this envelope structure.

Field Type Description id string System-generated unique event ID (UUID) sourceEventId string Original ID from the source system (for dedup). GitHub: Events API id. Jira: synthesized from issue key + changelog entry ID source string Source system identifier: "github" or "jira" eventSourceId string Slug of the event source that produced this event type string Normalized event type (e.g., issue.created, pr.merged) ref string Full URL uniquely identifying the subject of the event timestamp ISO-8601 When the event occurred in the source system actor Actor Who performed the action payload object Typed payload, schema determined by type sourceData object? Raw source-specific data escape hatch
