docs.title: Sharing dashboards
docs.text: Dashboards can be included in configuration packs. On the export page, select them in the Dashboards section. On import, dashboards are matched by name like other items: an existing dashboard with the same name is reported as a conflict. An imported dashboard becomes the default only if it was the default when exported and no dashboard is already the default.

docs.title: Logging and Debugging
docs.text: When something isn't working as expected — a workflow run fails, a task goes sideways, an event seems to be ignored, or a schedule trigger doesn't start a run — Axiom provides several layers of logging to help you trace what happened and why. This guide explains how to use them.

docs.title: The Processing Pipeline
docs.text:
Understanding Axiom's processing pipeline is the key to effective debugging. Every piece of work happens inside a workflow run, which is started or resumed along one of these paths:

Events:

Event Source polls → Event recorded in stream → Subscription filter matches → Routing rule fires
  → create-workflow (start a run) or workflow-dispatch (resume waiting runs)

Schedules:

Schedule trigger due → Fixed subject found or created → Run started (or skipped)

Runs:

Run starts → Nodes execute → Tasks created for action/human-task nodes → Agent or script executes

At each stage, Axiom records what happened. Debugging is a matter of finding where in the pipeline things went wrong and examining the logs at that stage.

docs.title: Where to Look: A Quick Reference
docs.text: Symptom Where to check first No events appearing at all Events > Event Sources > event source detail page > Poll Logs tab Events appear but no subscription matches Events > Subscriptions — use the Preview on the Filter tab to test the filter expression A subscription matched but no run started Event detail page > Processing tab — check the routing outcome (a skipped run means the subject already had an active run of that definition); confirm a create-workflow rule is configured A waiting run never received an event Confirm a workflow-dispatch rule matches the event and the receive-event node's event type and condition match A schedule trigger didn't start a run Workflow definition > Triggers tab — check Enabled, Next run, and Last outcome (skipped or failed: …) Workflow run stuck or failed Runs — open the run, check the current node, status, and failure reason Which runs did this event start? Event detail page > Runs tab A run failed and you fixed the cause Subject detail page > Runs tab > Re-run Task was created but failed Logs > Tasks — click View Log on the failed task Task completed but result is wrong Run detail page Overview tab (log link of the task) or subject Tasks tab > View Log No agent picks up a task Components > Agents — confirm an enabled agent's capabilities match action:<name> Want to see the full run tree for one workflow run Run detail page > Execution Trace tab, or Logs > Traces Want to see where a task or run came from and everything it led to Lineage panel (see below) Don't know where to start Logs > All Activity — scan the timeline

docs.title: All Activity Log
docs.text:
Logs > All Activity is the unified timeline of everything Axiom has done. This is the best starting point when you don't know where to look.

Every entry has a type label that tells you what happened, including:

Entry Type Meaning subject-created A new subject was created from an event workflow-started A workflow run began workflow-completed A workflow run finished successfully workflow-failed A workflow run failed workflow-cancelled A workflow run was cancelled task-started An agent began executing a task task-completed A task finished successfully task-failed A task failed task-awaiting-input The task requires human input (Inbox)

docs.title: Filtering the Activity Log
docs.text:
The activity log can be filtered with filter chips by:

  • Entry Type — show only workflow activity, only task activity, etc.
  • Summary — text search across activity summaries
  • Subject ID — show all activity for a specific subject
  • Event ID and Trace ID — show the activity of one event or one trace

docs.title: Viewing Execution Logs
docs.text: task-completed and task-failed entries have a View Log link to the task's execution log — the full AI agent output showing what the agent did.

docs.title: Step 1: Verify Events Are Being Received
docs.text:
Navigate to Events > Event Stream. This page shows every event that Axiom has recorded from its event sources. Each event shows:

  • Source — which event source produced it (e.g. github)
  • Type — the normalized event type (e.g. issue.created, pr.merged)
  • Ref — the full URL identifying the subject of the event
  • Timestamp — when the activity occurred in the source system

Narrow the list with filter chips for Event Type, Event Source, Ref and Actor (the exact login, case-insensitive). Clicking an event's type, source or actor label adds it as a filter.

Click any event row to open the event detail page. It has three tabs:

  • Event — the full typed payload. This is useful for verifying that the event source is producing the data you expect.
  • Processing — the event processing trail: one entry per subscription that evaluated the event, with its status, attempts and routing outcome (see Step 2).
  • Runs — the workflow runs started from this event, by routing rules or manually.

Use Run workflow… on the event detail page to start any published workflow from the event by hand, for example to test a workflow against a real event. See Triggering a Workflow.

If no events appear, check the event source configuration:

  1. Navigate to Events > Event Sources and click on the event source
  2. Check the Poll Logs tab — this shows the result of each poll cycle, including any errors
  3. Verify the event source is Enabled
  4. Verify the Authentication Secret is set and the token is valid
  5. Check the Poll Interval — a long interval means events may be delayed

docs.title: Step 2: Verify a Subscription Matched
docs.text:
If events are appearing in the stream but nothing downstream is happening, check Events > Subscriptions:

  1. Open the subscription you expect to match the event
  2. On the Filter tab, use Preview to test the filter expression against recent events and confirm it matches
  3. Verify the subscription is Enabled
  4. Check Process Events From — events that occurred before this cutoff are never evaluated against the subscription
  5. Confirm at least one routing rule is configured on the Routing tab with the type you expect (create-workflow or workflow-dispatch)

Each (event, subscription) pair is tracked in a processing ledger, shown on the event's Processing tab. Its status is skipped (filter didn't match), completed (routing succeeded), failed (routing threw an exception and will be retried), or exhausted (all attempts failed). A failed entry is retried with a growing delay, up to axiom.stream-pipeline.max-attempts attempts in total (default 3). The entry shows its attempts, last attempt and next retry; use Retry now (or Retry once more for an exhausted entry) to retry immediately. A create-workflow rule whose subject already has an active run of the same definition completes with a skipped run item in its routing outcome — no run is queued.

docs.title: Step 3: Check the Run
docs.text:
Open the Runs page and filter by subject, workflow, status or label. The run detail page shows:

  • On the Overview tab: the run's status, any failure reason, the triggering event, the events that resumed it, its inputs and labels, and the tasks created by its nodes with their output and log
  • On the Diagram tab: where the run is in the graph — whether it's waiting on a timer (wait node), an external event (receive-event node), or a human response (human-task node, visible in the Inbox)
  • On the Timeline tab: the nodes the run passed through, in order
  • On the Execution Trace tab: the run's trace (see Using Traces)

If you fix the cause of a failed run, start it again with Re-run on the subject's Runs tab. See Re-running a Failed Run.

See Workflows for the full authoring and run-time reference.

docs.title: Step 4: Check the Task
docs.text:
Navigate to Logs > Tasks. This page shows all tasks across all subjects, with:

  • Action Type — which action type was used
  • Subject — link to the subject
  • Status — Pending, InProgress, Completed, Failed, AwaitingInput, etc.

Click View Log on a completed or failed task to see the full execution log — the AI agent's conversation, tool calls, and output. This tells you exactly what the agent did (or tried to do).

Common task issues:

  • Failed — check the execution log for errors. Common causes: tool script failures, agent subprocess timeouts, missing secrets.
  • Pending — no matching agent is idle. Check Components > Agents for an enabled agent whose capabilities match action:<action-type-name>.
  • AwaitingInput — the task needs a human response. Navigate to the Inbox to respond.

docs.title: Tracing Schedule Triggers
docs.text:
Open the workflow definition and go to the Triggers tab. Each schedule trigger shows:

  • Next run — when it fires next (empty while disabled). Cron expressions are evaluated in UTC.
  • Last run and Last outcome — started, skipped (the fixed subject already had an active run of this definition), or failed: <reason>

Runs started by a schedule trigger carry the label trigger: schedule, so you can find them on the Runs page with the label filter trigger:schedule, or open the trigger's fixed subject to see its run timeline.

docs.title: Using the Subject Detail Page
docs.text: The subject detail page brings together all the information about a single subject. Navigate to Subjects and click on a subject.

docs.title: Runs Tab
docs.text: A list of every workflow run on the subject, active and past, newest first. Click a run to open its detail page. Failed runs have a Re-run button that starts a new run of the latest published version of the workflow with the same title, labels and inputs (see Re-running a Failed Run).

docs.title: Tasks Tab
docs.text: Shows every task created by runs on this subject. Each task lists its action type, assigned agent, status, and timestamps. Click View Log on any completed or failed task to see exactly what the agent did, or Lineage to see where the task came from.

docs.title: Thread Tab
docs.text: The thread is a chronological narrative of everything that happened on the subject. Each entry has an author type (agent, user, or system) and an entry type (task-result, event, etc.). The content is rendered as Markdown.

docs.title: Events Tab
docs.text: Shows all stream events (from event sources) that were associated with this subject.

docs.title: Following the Chain of Work (Lineage)
docs.text:
The Lineage panel shows the chain of work an item belongs to, so you do not have to hop between the event, trace, workflow run, task and usage pages. It is available on:

  • the event detail page (Lineage tab),
  • the workflow run detail page (Lineage tab),
  • the Logs > Tasks page and the subject Tasks tab (Lineage button on each task).

The panel has two views:

  • Show origin walks back to what caused the item, for example task ← workflow run ← event.
  • Show results walks forward to what the item produced, for example event → workflow run → tasks.

Every item links to its own page and shows its status and its direct AI cost; the total AI cost of the items shown is displayed below the tree. Items whose records were removed by data retention are shown in italics as "deleted or unavailable". Very large chains are cut off after a fixed number of levels and items; the panel says so when this happens.

docs.title: Using Traces
docs.text: While the activity log, event stream, and task log each show one dimension of what happened, a trace shows the complete tree structure of a single workflow run. Traces answer the question: "What exactly happened, in what order, and how long did each step take?"

docs.title: When to Use Traces vs. the Activity Log
docs.text:
• Use the Activity Log when you want a timeline view across multiple events and subjects — "what has the system been doing?"
  • Use a Trace when you want to drill into one specific run — "what happened step by step for this workflow run?"

docs.title: Accessing Traces
docs.text:
• Logs > Traces — browse all traces, with filter chips for type and status
  • The workflow run detail page's Execution Trace tab — the trace of that run
  • The Logs > All Activity page — the Trace column links each entry to its trace, and the subject Tasks tab has a Trace column for each task

docs.title: Reading the Trace Graph
docs.text:
The trace detail page renders the node tree as a left-to-right interactive tree:

  • Nodes represent pipeline steps — each shows an icon, a status label, a summary, and timing information
  • Edges connect parent nodes to their children, showing the execution flow
  • Node color reflects status: green for completed, blue for in-progress, red for failed

docs.title: Viewing Node Details
docs.text: Click any node in the graph to open a detail view. The content depends on the node's referenced entity type — for example, an event node shows the raw event payload, a task node shows action type/agent/status/output, and a tool-execution node shows the full JSON input and output. The tool execution detail is especially useful for debugging — you can see exactly what data each tool received and returned.

docs.title: Real-Time Updates
docs.text: When a trace is still in progress, the graph updates automatically as new nodes are added. You don't need to refresh the page — the UI receives server-sent events (SSE) and re-renders the graph when the trace changes.

docs.title: Debugging Checklist
docs.text:
When something isn't working, work through the pipeline in order:

  1. Is the event source polling? Check the event source detail page > Poll Logs tab.
  2. Are events being recorded? Check Events > Event Stream.
  3. Does a subscription match? Check Events > Subscriptions and use Preview.
  4. Did the routing rule fire? Check the event's Processing tab for the ledger status and routing outcome of that (event, subscription) pair — including skipped run items — and its Runs tab, or look for the run on the Runs page.
  5. For schedules, did the trigger fire? Check the Triggers tab's last outcome.
  6. Where is the run? Open the run and check its current node, status, and failure reason.
  7. Was an agent available? Check Components > Agents — is there an enabled agent with matching capabilities?
  8. Did the task execute? Check Logs > Tasks or the run's tasks. Read the execution log.
  9. Did the tools work? The task execution log shows each tool call and its output. If a tool failed, check its script template under Components > Tools.
  10. Were secrets available? Secrets are not injected automatically. If an action type or one of its tools needs API credentials, check that the secret exists under Components > Secrets and that the action type's Environment declares it (for example GH_TOKEN=${secret:GH_TOKEN}).

Use a Trace for the Full Picture

For any workflow run, opening its trace gives you the entire run tree in one view — every step, every tool call. This is often faster than checking each log page individually, especially when you need to understand the relationship between steps.

docs.title: Navigating the UI
docs.text: Axiom's web interface is organized around a sidebar navigation, a top masthead, and a central content area. This guide gives you a quick tour of the UI so you know where to find things.

docs.title: Masthead
docs.text:
The masthead runs across the top of every page. It contains:

  • Apitomy Axiom — click the title to return to the Runs page (the landing page) from any page
  • Robot icon — opens the AI Assistant (visible only when at least one registered agent supports interactive sessions)
  • Theme toggle — cycles between light, dark, and system theme
  • Question mark icon — opens the About dialog showing the application version, active AI engine, and links to the source repository

docs.title: Dashboards
docs.text: Axiom supports multiple user-configurable dashboards, each with tabs of widgets chosen from a built-in catalog. Dashboards in the sidebar (/dashboards) opens the default dashboard, or the dashboards list when no dashboard is the default. See Dashboards for every widget and its settings.

docs.title: Dashboard List
docs.text:
The dashboards list (/dashboards/all) shows all dashboards with their name, labels, number of widgets and last update. From here you can:

  • Create Dashboard: create an empty dashboard with a name, description and optional labels
  • Create from Template: create a dashboard from the Operations, Event Operations or AI Usage template
  • Set as default: click the star icon (only one dashboard can be the default)
  • Delete: remove a dashboard after confirming

When there are no dashboards, the list offers the templates directly. Click a dashboard to open it.

docs.title: Dashboard View
docs.text:
Each dashboard shows its widgets on a responsive grid. All dashboards returns to the list and Refresh reloads every widget. The view has two modes:

  • Normal mode (default): widgets are read-only and the layout is locked
  • Edit mode: click Edit to drag and resize widgets, change a widget's settings (gear icon), remove widgets (X icon), manage tabs, and edit the dashboard's name, description and labels

In edit mode, Add Widget opens the widget catalog, grouped by category (Runs, Inbox, Events, AI & Cost, System and Subjects).

docs.title: Dashboard Labels
docs.text: Dashboard labels are subject labels. Widgets that show subject-related data (runs, tasks, activity, subjects and AI usage) only include subjects with those labels. Widgets for event sources, subscriptions, schedules and system health are global and ignore them. When a dashboard has labels, each widget shows a Filtered or Global badge.

docs.title: Sidebar Navigation
docs.text: The sidebar lists, in order: Runs, Subjects, Inbox, Dashboards, the Events section (Event Sources, Subscriptions, Event Stream), Workbench, and the Logs, Metrics, Components and Settings sections.

docs.title: Runs
docs.text: Runs is the landing page (/runs). It lists every workflow run across all subjects with its status, start time and duration. The Run column names each run as <subject> — <workflow> v<version>, with the run's title below it when the run has one. Filter chips narrow the list by Status, Workflow (name or ID), Subject ID, and Label (key:value; add several labels to require all of them). Clicking a run's status adds it as a filter. Click anywhere else on a row to open the run's detail page, which shows the workflow graph with the current node highlighted, the run's resolved standard inputs (the subject; the event is shown as the triggering event instead) and labels, the triggering event, the tasks created by its nodes (with their outputs), and a Cancel button for active runs. See Workflows.

docs.title: Subjects
docs.text:
The Subjects page lists all subjects with their name, derived active state, ref, labels, and last update. A subject is active when it has a running or waiting workflow run. You can filter by name or labels.

Click any subject to open its detail page, which has several tabs:

  • Runs — a timeline of every workflow run on this subject, active and past. Failed runs have a Re-run button; see Re-running a Failed Run
  • Body — the subject's Markdown body
  • Tasks — all tasks created by runs on this subject, with status and execution details
  • Thread — a chronological log of everything that happened on the subject (events received, task results, notes)
  • Events — raw stream events from event sources associated with this subject
  • Metrics — AI cost, token usage, and disk usage for this subject

From the subject detail page you can also edit labels and delete the subject.

docs.title: Inbox
docs.text: The Inbox page shows tasks with status AwaitingInput — tasks created by workflow human-task nodes that are waiting for a person. A badge on the sidebar shows the count of pending items. Click any item to review its context and respond; the waiting workflow run then resumes.

docs.title: Dashboards
docs.text: See Dashboards above.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
The Events section covers the event pipeline described in Events and Subscriptions:

Page What it shows Event Sources Configured event sources to GitHub/Jira, their poll status, and poll log history Subscriptions Filtered, routed views over the event stream (create-workflow and workflow-dispatch rules) — create, edit, and preview filter expressions here Event Stream Every normalized event Axiom has recorded from its event sources. Filter chips narrow it by Event Type, Event Source, Ref and Actor (exact login, case-insensitive); clicking a type, source or actor in a row adds it as a filter. Click a row to open the event.

The event detail page shows the full typed payload (Event tab), how subscriptions processed it (Processing tab), and the runs started from it (Runs tab). Run workflow… starts a run of any published workflow with the event, listing suggested workflows first; such runs get the label trigger:manual.

docs.title: Workbench
docs.text: The Workbench (/workbench) lists compositions. Open one to design a workflow together with its action types and tools, with an AI Assistant chat beside the canvas, test script and Node.js items, review the composition's runs, and publish the drafts. See Workbench.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
The Logs section has several sub-pages, each showing a different slice of system activity:

Page What it shows All Activity Unified feed of all system events — subject creation, workflow runs, task execution Tasks Task execution history — which agent ran what action type, duration, cost, and outcome Traces Browse and filter workflow run execution traces

Each log page supports filtering and pagination.

The Traces page deserves special mention. While the other log pages show tabular data, a trace detail page renders the node tree as an interactive tree. Each node represents a step in the run (node entered, task created, tool executed, etc.) and is color-coded by status. Click any node to open a detail view showing the full data for that step, including tool input/output for tool executions.

You can also navigate to a trace directly from a workflow run or a subject's tasks.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
The Metrics section has two sub-pages:

Page What it shows AI Usage Token costs broken down by invocation type, action type, and date range. Shows summary totals at the top. Disk Usage Workspace storage consumed by each subject's workspace. Shows total disk usage and per-subject breakdown.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
The Components section contains workflows and the building blocks they and the AI Assistant use:

Page Purpose Action Types Define the kinds of work that workflow action nodes run — execution mode (agent, script or Node.js), prompt, script or code template, inputs and outputs, allowed tools, and model/engine overrides Agents Register AI agent slots with capabilities that determine which work they're eligible for AI Assistant (Session Templates) Define AI Assistant session templates with system prompts, agent type, tools, and MCP servers MCP Servers Register external MCP tool servers (HTTP or stdio) Secrets Store encrypted credentials; processes receive only the secrets their environment declares Tools Define script-based tools with parameters and bash templates Toolsets Group tools into named collections for reuse Workflows Workflow definitions (/components/workflows); each detail page has the Design, Versions, Runs and Triggers (schedule triggers) tabs. See Workflows

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
The Settings section contains instance-wide configuration:

Page Purpose AI Engine View and change the default agent type, health checks, and available models per registered agent Data Retention Configure how long inactive subjects, traces, events, workflow runs, activity and AI usage are kept before automatic cleanup (0 keeps history forever) Configuration Packs Export and import bundles of configuration as JSON

Most configuration pages follow the same pattern: a list view with a Create button, and a detail page with tabbed sections for editing. Changes on detail pages are not saved until you click Save Changes.

docs.title: Common Patterns
docs.text:
A few interactions work the same way throughout the UI:

  • Filtering — list pages have a filter bar where you can add filter criteria by type (name, status, labels). Active filters appear as removable chips below the toolbar.
  • Pagination — large lists are paginated. Use the controls in the toolbar to change page size or navigate between pages.
  • Clickable rows — table rows are clickable and navigate to the item's detail page.
  • Labels — many items support labels for organization. Clicking a label chip in a table adds it as a filter. Labels can be edited from detail pages.
  • Delete confirmation — destructive actions always show a confirmation dialog before proceeding.
  • Real-time updates — the UI receives server-sent events (SSE) for live updates. Activity feeds, run and task statuses update automatically without refreshing the page.

docs.title: Usage Examples
docs.text:
This section walks through two end-to-end examples showing how to configure Axiom for real-world use cases. Each example explains the goal, lists every configuration item needed, and provides the exact values to enter.

If you haven't read the Concepts guide yet, start there — it explains the building blocks referenced below.

docs.title: Example 1: Automatically Label New GitHub Issues
Goal
docs.text:
When a new issue is opened on a monitored GitHub repository, an AI agent reads the issue title and body, examines the repository's available labels, chooses the most relevant ones, and applies them — all automatically.

This example uses a Subscription with a create-workflow routing rule that starts a Workflow whose single action node runs an Action Type in agent mode. The action type allows three custom Tools that encapsulate the GitHub CLI commands. The AI agent can only call these three tools, ensuring it can read issue details and apply labels but nothing else.

docs.title: What You'll Configure
docs.text: Item Purpose Secret GitHub API token for authentication Event Source Polls a GitHub repository for new activity 3 Tools Fetch labels, fetch issue details, apply labels Action Type Defines the auto-labeling behavior and prompt Workflow Runs the action type on the issue's subject Subscription Starts the workflow for each new issue Agent An AI agent slot to execute the task

docs.title: Step 1: Create a Secret
docs.text:
Navigate to Components > Secrets and add a secret:

Field Value Name GH_TOKEN Description GitHub personal access token Value Your GitHub PAT with repo scope

This token is encrypted at rest and injected as an environment variable into AI agent subprocesses, where the gh CLI picks it up automatically.

docs.title: Step 2: Add an Event Source
docs.text:
Navigate to Events > Event Sources and click Add Event Source:

Field Value ID e.g. github-com Name e.g. My Repository Source Type GitHub Base URL https://github.com Repositories your-org/your-repo Enabled Yes Poll Interval 60 (seconds) Authentication Secret GH_TOKEN

Axiom will now poll this repository every 60 seconds for new issues, pull requests, comments, and other activity, and record it in the event stream.

docs.title: Step 3: Create Three Tools
docs.text: Navigate to Components > Tools and create each of the following tools. For each one, click Create Tool, enter the name, then configure the description, parameters, and script template on the detail page.

docs.title: Tool: fetch_github_labels
docs.text:
Lists all labels available on a repository. The AI agent uses this to know which labels it can choose from.

Info tab:

Field Value Name fetch_github_labels Description List all labels available on a GitHub repository

Parameters tab — add one parameter:

Name Type Required Description repository string Yes Repository in owner/repo format

Script Template tab:

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
gh label list --repo "{{repository}}" --json name,description --limit 100

docs.title: Tool: fetch_github_issue
docs.text:
Fetches the title, body, and current labels of a specific issue. The AI agent uses this to understand what the issue is about.

Info tab:

Field Value Name fetch_github_issue Description Fetch the title, body, and current labels of a GitHub issue

Parameters tab — add one parameter:

Name Type Required Description issue_url string Yes Full URL of the issue

Script Template tab:

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
gh issue view "{{issue_url}}" --json title,body,labels

The gh CLI accepts a full issue URL anywhere it accepts an issue reference, so this tool works directly with the ref value Axiom passes to the agent.

docs.title: Tool: apply_github_labels
docs.text:
Adds labels to an issue. This is the only write operation the AI agent can perform.

Info tab:

Field Value Name apply_github_labels Description Add one or more labels to a GitHub issue

Parameters tab — add two parameters:

Name Type Required Description issue_url string Yes Full URL of the issue labels string Yes Comma-separated list of label names to apply

Script Template tab:

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
gh issue edit "{{issue_url}}" --add-label "{{labels}}"

docs.title: Step 4: Create the Action Type
docs.text:
Navigate to Components > Action Types and click Create Action Type:

Field Value Name Auto-Label Issue Execution Mode Agent — AI agent

On the detail page, configure the remaining fields:

Info tab:

Field Value Description Analyze a new GitHub issue and apply relevant labels

Inputs tab — declare what the action operates on:

Name Type Required Description ref string Yes URL of the issue to label repository string Yes Repository in owner/repo format

Allowed Tools tab — add exactly these three tools:

fetch_github_labels
fetch_github_issue
apply_github_labels

Prompt Template tab:

You are a GitHub issue labeling assistant. A new issue has been created and your job
is to apply the most relevant labels from the repository's existing label set.

## Instructions

1. Fetch the issue details using the `fetch_github_issue` tool with issue URL
   `{{inputs.ref}}`.

2. Fetch the available labels using the `fetch_github_labels` tool with repository
   `{{inputs.repository}}`.

3. Based on the issue title and body, select the most relevant labels from the
   available set. Choose labels that accurately categorize the issue. Typically
   1-3 labels is appropriate. Do not invent new labels — only use labels that
   exist in the repository.

4. Apply the selected labels using the `apply_github_labels` tool with issue URL
   `{{inputs.ref}}`.

If the issue already has appropriate labels, or if no labels clearly apply, do not
make any changes.

docs.title: Step 5: Create the Workflow
docs.text:
Navigate to Components > Workflows and click Create Workflow Definition with the name Auto-Label New Issues. The new definition is scaffolded with a Start node (declaring subject and event) connected to an End node. In the editor:

  1. Drag an Auto-Label Issue action node from the palette (every action type appears there) between Start and End
  2. Double-click the action node to open its properties and map its inputs from the run context: ref ← context.subject.ref and repository ← context.subject.repository
  3. Connect Start → Auto-Label Issue → End
  4. Click Publish

Using the Workbench

You can also build the workflow, the action type and the tools together in the Workbench, with the AI Assistant's help, and publish them in one step.

docs.title: Step 6: Add a Subscription
docs.text:
Navigate to Events > Subscriptions and click Add Subscription with the name Label new issues. Then configure it on the detail page:

Field Value Filter Expression event.type == 'issue.created' Enabled Yes

Under Routing Rules, add one rule of type Create Workflow and select the Auto-Label New Issues definition. Use the Preview on the subscription page to confirm the filter matches the events you expect, then click Save Changes.

docs.title: Step 7: Ensure a Matching Agent Exists
docs.text:
Navigate to Components > Agents. You need at least one enabled agent whose capabilities match this action type. A new installation already has four agents with capability *. If none exist, click Create Agent:

Field Value Name e.g. AI Agent Type Claude Code (or your preferred agent type)

Then add the capability * on the agent's Capabilities tab.

A capability of * matches any work, including the action:Auto-Label Issue capability this task will request. See AI Agents for how capability matching works.

docs.title: How It Works End to End
docs.text:
1. Someone opens a new issue on the monitored repository
  2. The Event Source detects the new issue on its next poll and records it in the event stream
  3. The Subscription's filter matches the issue.created event, and its create-workflow rule finds or creates a subject for the issue's URL and starts an Auto-Label New Issues run on it
  4. The run reaches the action node, which creates a Task leased by an available agent whose capabilities match action:Auto-Label Issue
  5. The agent reads the issue, checks available labels, picks the best matches, and applies them
  6. The task completes, the run finishes, and the result is visible on the Runs page and on the subject's detail page

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
Every Monday, summarize all GitHub issues and pull requests where you were @mentioned in the past 7 days, organized by repository, and post the summary to a dedicated subject so the history of weekly summaries accumulates in one place.

This example uses a Workflow with a Schedule Trigger. The workflow's action node runs an Action Type whose agent calls a custom Tool that queries the GitHub notifications API, then posts the summary to the subject's thread with the axiom_add_thread_entry SDK function.

docs.title: What You'll Configure
docs.text: Item Purpose Secret GitHub API token for authentication Tool Queries GitHub notifications API for @mentions Action Type Defines the summary prompt and allowed tools Workflow + Schedule Trigger Runs the action type every Monday on a fixed subject Agent An AI agent slot to execute the task

docs.title: Step 1: Create a Secret
docs.text:
If you already created a GH_TOKEN secret (e.g. from Example 1), skip this step.

Navigate to Components > Secrets and add:

Field Value Name GH_TOKEN Description GitHub personal access token Value Your GitHub PAT with notifications scope

docs.title: Step 2: Create the Tool
docs.text: Navigate to Components > Tools and click Create Tool with the name github_mentions. Then configure it on the detail page:

docs.title: Tool: github_mentions
docs.text:
Queries the GitHub notifications API for all @mention notifications since a given date.

Info tab:

Field Value Name github_mentions Description Fetch all GitHub @mention notifications since a given date

Parameters tab — add one parameter:

Name Type Required Description since string Yes ISO date (e.g. 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z)

Script Template tab:

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
gh api /notifications \
  -X GET \
  -f all=true \
  -f since="{{since}}" \
  --jq '[.[] | select(.reason == "mention") | {
    repo: .repository.full_name,
    title: .subject.title,
    type: .subject.type,
    url: .subject.url,
    updated: .updated_at
  }]'

This script uses the GitHub notifications API with reason == "mention" to filter for only @mentions. The since parameter limits results to the summary's time window.

docs.title: Step 3: Create the Action Type
docs.text:
Navigate to Components > Action Types and click Create Action Type with the name Summarize @Mentions and execution mode Agent — AI agent. On the detail page:

Allowed Tools tab — add the tool and the SDK functions used to find the subject and post to its thread:

github_mentions
mcp__axiom-sdk__axiom_list_subjects
mcp__axiom-sdk__axiom_add_thread_entry

Inputs tab — add a required subjectName input (string, "Name of the subject to post the summary to").

Prompt Template tab:

Summarize all GitHub @mentions from the past 7 days.

1. Compute the date 7 days ago (ISO 8601, UTC) and run the `github_mentions` tool with
   that value as `since`.
2. Produce a Markdown summary with:
   - Total number of mentions, repositories involved, and a breakdown by type (Issue vs PR)
   - For each repository (alphabetically), each mention with its title, type, and date
     (newest first) and a one-line note on whether it likely needs a response
   - An "Action Items" section listing mentions that need follow-up (or "None")
3. Find the ID of the subject named "{{inputs.subjectName}}" with `axiom_list_subjects`, then post
   the summary to that subject's thread with `axiom_add_thread_entry`.

docs.title: Step 4: Create the Workflow and Schedule Trigger
docs.text:
Navigate to Components > Workflows, create a workflow definition named Weekly @Mentions, add a Summarize @Mentions action node between Start and End, map its subjectName input from context.subject.name, and remove the event input from the Start node (a schedule trigger has no event, so a required event would stop every firing), and click Publish.

On the workflow's Triggers tab, add a schedule trigger:

Field Value Cron 0 8 * * 1 (Mondays at 08:00 UTC) Subject name Weekly @Mentions Enabled Yes

docs.title: Step 5: Ensure a Matching Agent Exists
docs.text: Navigate to Components > Agents and confirm at least one enabled agent's capabilities match action:Summarize @Mentions. A capability of * or action:* matches any action type.

docs.title: How It Works End to End
docs.text:
1. Every Monday at 08:00 UTC, the schedule trigger fires
  2. On the first firing, Axiom creates the Weekly @Mentions subject (ref schedule:Weekly @Mentions); later firings reuse it
  3. A Weekly @Mentions run starts on that subject — unless the previous week's run is somehow still active, in which case the firing is skipped and the trigger's last outcome shows skipped
  4. The action node creates a task; an agent matching action:Summarize @Mentions is leased from the pool
  5. The agent calls github_mentions, organizes the results, and posts the summary to the subject's thread
  6. Each week's summary is visible on the subject's detail page, alongside the timeline of past runs

docs.title: Workflow Workbench
docs.text:
The Workflow Workbench is a place to build a workflow together with the action types and tools it uses, with an AI assistant working beside you. You edit drafts. Nothing you or the AI change in the workbench affects the running system until you publish it.

Open it from Workbench in the sidebar (after Events).

docs.title: Compositions
docs.text: A composition groups one workflow with the action types and tools you build for it. Each item in a composition is a draft with its own revision history.

docs.title: The composition list
docs.text:
The Workbench page (/workbench) lists your compositions with these columns:

Column Meaning Name The composition name. Goal The optional goal you entered when creating it. State AI working while the AI assistant is running a turn, else idle. Updated When the composition last changed.

Click a row to open the composition. Use the trash icon on a row to delete a composition (you are asked to confirm).

docs.title: Creating a composition
docs.text:
1. Click New composition.
  2. Enter a Name (required) and, optionally, a Goal that describes what the workflow should do.
  3. Click Create.

The composition is created with a blank workflow draft that has the same name, and the workbench opens.

docs.title: Drafts and published items
docs.text: Every item in a composition is a draft. A draft can be new, or a copy of an existing published action type or tool that you added to the composition. Drafts with changes that are not yet published are shown in blue in the Components tree (hover text "Unpublished changes"). Use Publish… to make drafts live (see Publishing).

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
The workbench page (/workbench/:id) has a toolbar and three panes:

  • Components (left): the composition tree.
  • Centre: tabs with the workflow canvas and the action type and tool editors, and a bottom panel with the Tests and Runs tabs.
  • AI Assistant (right): the chat with the AI.

docs.title: Toolbar
docs.text: Control What it does Breadcrumb (Workbench / name) Goes back to the composition list. Apply live / Review changes How AI workflow changes reach the canvas (see Working with the AI). Saved per composition. Place new nodes / Tidy after AI changes How the canvas lays out AI changes: place only the new nodes, or tidy the whole layout. Maximize canvas / Restore side panels Collapses (or restores) both side panes. Focus / Exit focus (Ctrl+Shift+F) Hides the application masthead and sidebar. Break out Opens the composition in a new browser window without the application chrome. The original window shows "Opened in another window" with a Bring back here link. Publish… Saves any pending edits and opens the Publish dialog.

docs.title: Resizing and collapsing panes
docs.text:
Drag the splitters between the panes to resize the side panes (160 to 800 pixels). Use the « and » buttons to collapse or expand the left pane and the chat pane. While the chat pane is collapsed, a pulsing marker shows when the AI is working.

The bottom panel is collapsed when you open a composition. Use the arrow button on its header to expand it. It expands by itself when a test run starts, when the AI suggests a test, or when a new run of the workflow fails.

Pane widths, collapsed panes, the layout option and the selected bottom tab are stored in the browser.

docs.title: Components
docs.text: The Components pane lists the composition's items in four groups: Workflow, Action types, Tools and Subscriptions (see Subscriptions). Click an item to open it in a centre tab.

docs.title: Adding action types and tools
docs.text:
Click the Create (plus) button in the pane toolbar and choose Action Type or Tool. In the dialog, choose:

  • New: enter a Name. For a new action type, also choose the Execution mode:
  • AI Agent — executed by an AI agent.
  • Node.js — runs a JavaScript module.
  • Script — executes a bash script.
  • Existing: pick a published action type or tool. A draft copy of it is added to the composition.

Click Add. The new item opens in a tab.

You can also add an action type from the workflow canvas: when you open an action type referenced by a node, the workbench opens its draft, or adds it to the composition (as a copy of the published action type if one exists, otherwise as a new draft).

docs.title: Row menu
docs.text:
Each action type and tool row has a menu (three dots) with:

  • Test… — opens the test dialog for the item (see Testing).
  • Ask AI about this… — pre-fills the chat with a question about the item. Disabled while the AI is working.
  • Remove — removes the draft from the composition after confirmation. Its draft and revision history are discarded; a published item with the same name is not deleted. If the item is still used, the dialog lists where. Disabled while the AI is working.

The workflow has no row menu and cannot be removed.

docs.title: Markers
docs.text:
Each row can show:

  • A status icon: a green check (valid), a yellow warning (warnings; publishing is still allowed) or a red error (errors; fix them before publishing). Hover for the number of problems.
  • A lock icon while the AI is editing the item. The item becomes editable when the AI turn ends.
  • An AI label on items changed by the last AI turn.

docs.title: Revision history
docs.text: Select an item and click Revision history (clock icon) in the pane toolbar. The dialog lists the item's revisions, newest first, with the author (AI or You), the AI turn id, and the time. The current revision is marked Current. Click Restore to make an older revision the current one.

docs.title: Editing
docs.text: All editors save automatically shortly after you stop typing. If an item was changed elsewhere in the meantime, the editor shows a "Changed elsewhere" warning with a Reload link.

docs.title: Workflow canvas
docs.text:
The first centre tab is the workflow canvas. It cannot be closed. It is the same Flow editor described in Workflows, with these differences:

  • Node and edge properties open in a properties dialog: double-click a node or edge.
  • Simulate is turned off.
  • The right-click menu of nodes, edges and the canvas has Ask AI about this…, and the menu of a problem has Ask AI to fix this. Both pre-fill the chat.
  • The canvas validates the workflow against the composition, so action types that exist only as drafts in the composition are known to the editor.

docs.title: Action type and tool editors
docs.text:
Action types and tools open in their own tabs with the same editors as the Components pages (for example Info, Inputs, Outputs, Script or Code, Environment for action types; Info, Parameters, Script Template for tools). When an item has problems, its Problems tab offers Ask AI to fix this on each problem.

Close an item tab with its close button or by middle-clicking the tab.

docs.title: Working with the AI
docs.text:
The AI Assistant pane is a chat with an AI that works on the same drafts as you. The pane title shows a badge with the engine and model in use (for example OpenCode · default); hover over it for details. If the assistant cannot start, the pane shows "Assistant unavailable" with a Retry link.

When you send a message, the workbench first saves your pending workflow edits and tells the AI which nodes and edges are selected on the canvas. While the AI is working, the chat input is disabled and the items it edits are locked for you. Clearing the conversation (/clear) is not supported in the workbench.

docs.title: Applying AI workflow changes
docs.text:
The AI changes the workflow by proposing change sets. They are applied by your canvas when the AI turn ends:

  • Apply live: the changes are applied to the canvas directly.
  • Review changes: the changes are shown on the canvas as a proposal that you accept or reject.

If a change set cannot be applied (for example because the workflow changed in the meantime), the canvas shows an error. The AI changes action types and tools directly; those changes appear in their tabs.

docs.title: Tool cards
docs.text: The AI's tool calls are shown as compact cards in the chat, for example "Read the composition", "Created action type check-pr-status VALID" or "Proposed 1 workflow change". Click a card to open the item it is about, go to the workflow, or open a suggested test. Expand a card to see the details of the call.

docs.title: Asking the AI about something
docs.text:
Several places pre-fill the chat with a prompt that you can edit before sending:

  • Ask AI about this… in a component row menu or the canvas context menu.
  • Ask AI to fix this on a problem in the canvas or an item editor.
  • Ask AI to analyze on a failed workflow run (see Runs).

docs.title: Undoing an AI turn
docs.text: After an AI turn ends, an Undo AI turn button appears in the chat toolbar. It restores the items the turn changed and removes the items it created, then shows a summary (restored, removed, skipped). If you changed the workflow after that turn, the workflow is left alone.

docs.title: What the AI can and cannot do
docs.text:
The AI can:

  • Read the composition and its items, and create, update and remove action type, tool and subscription drafts.
  • Change the workflow, only through change sets.
  • Validate the composition.
  • Look at recent events in the Event Stream and evaluate expressions against them.
  • Preview a subscription filter against the 200 most recent events (preview_subscription).
  • Read runs of the published workflow and their traces.
  • Look up published action types, tools and secret names (never secret values).
  • Suggest a test with sample inputs.

The AI cannot publish or enable subscriptions, and it never runs tests or workflows. When it creates or changes a Node.js or script action type or a tool, it suggests a test that you can run.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: You can test Node.js and script action types and tools from the workbench. AI Agent action types cannot be tested yet. Only you run tests.

docs.title: Running a test
docs.text:
Start a test in one of these ways:

  • Open the item's tab and click Test… in the bottom panel header.
  • Choose Test… in the item's row menu.

The test dialog asks for the item's inputs (for an action type) or parameters (for a tool). Each field shows its type and description; required fields are marked. Object and array values are entered as JSON. Under Subject, choose a subject to run in its directory, or None — run in a temporary directory. For a tool, the Environment section sets the variables for the test run: a tool gets no secrets automatically, so add the secrets it needs (in a workflow it runs with the environment of the action type that allows it). An action type uses its own Environment. Click Run. The workbench remembers the values (and a tool's environment) you used for each item.

The test uses the current draft, including unsaved edits, which are saved first.

docs.title: The Tests tab
docs.text: The Tests tab of the bottom panel lists recent test runs, newest first. Each row shows a status icon (running, passed, failed, error or suggested), the item name (click it to open the item), the time, duration, exit code and a one-line summary. Click a row to open the test run details.

docs.title: Test run details
docs.text:
The details dialog opens when a run starts and updates when it finishes. It shows any problems, then these tabs:

  • Script or Code: the resolved script or Node.js code that ran.
  • Inputs or Parameters: the values used, as a list or JSON.
  • Outputs: the outputs of an action type.
  • Stdout/err: the standard output and error streams.

docs.title: AI-suggested tests
docs.text: When the AI suggests a test, it appears in the Tests tab with a Suggested by AI label and a Run… button. Run… opens the test dialog pre-filled with the AI's sample values. Review them before you click Run; a test runs the real code against real systems.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Only Node.js and script action types, and tools, can be tested.
  • At most 2 test runs per composition can run at the same time.
  • Standard output and standard error are each truncated to 64,000 characters.
  • Tool test runs time out after 30 seconds.
  • The last 50 test runs of each composition are kept in memory. They are lost when the server restarts.

docs.title: Runs
docs.text:
The Runs tab of the bottom panel lists the runs of the composition's published workflow, newest first. Until the workflow is published, the tab shows "Publish the workflow to see its runs here." Use Refresh to reload the list.

Each row shows the status, run number, subject (followed by the run's title when it has one), workflow version, start time and, for failed or waiting runs, the current node. Failed runs have an Ask AI to analyze link.

Click a row to open the run details dialog. It shows the status, version, start time, duration and current node, the failure reason, and these tabs:

  • Graph: the workflow with the run's progress.
  • Failure (failed runs only): the failed tasks with their output or log.
  • Context: the run context as JSON.

For a failed run, Ask AI to analyze pre-fills the chat with a request to find the cause and fix the workflow or its components. Open run page opens the run in the Runs page in a new tab.

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text:
Click Publish… to open the Publish dialog. It lists the items with unpublished changes. Items without errors are selected by default. When you select an item, the changed drafts it depends on are selected too (the action types a workflow uses, and the tools an action type uses) and marked "required by".

Click Publish. The workbench then:

  • Blocks the publish if a selected item has validation errors, or uses an action type or tool that is neither published nor selected. The dialog lists the problems per item. Warnings do not block publishing.
  • Reports a conflict if a published item changed outside the workbench since it was loaded, if a new item's name is already used by a published item, or if an item was renamed (publishing creates a new item and keeps the old one). Click Publish anyway to publish regardless.
  • Otherwise, creates or updates the published workflow, action types, tools and subscriptions, and reports how many were created and updated.

Publishing does not delete published items (removed drafts and old names stay published) and does not start the workflow. Published subscriptions stay disabled until you enable them (see Subscriptions).

docs.title: Subscriptions
docs.text:
A composition can own the subscriptions that drive its workflow, so the workbench takes you from a goal to working automation. A subscription filters the Event Stream and routes matching events (see Concepts). In a composition, a subscription can:

  • Start runs of the composition's workflow, with a create-workflow rule. The rule must name the composition's own workflow (workflowDefinitionName).
  • Feed receive-event nodes, with a workflow-dispatch rule, which delivers events to runs waiting at a matching receive-event node. Without a workflow-dispatch subscription, receive-event nodes never receive events.

docs.title: Creating a subscription
docs.text: Click the Create (plus) button in the Components pane toolbar and choose Subscription, or ask the AI to create one. A composition can have any number of subscriptions.

docs.title: The subscription editor
docs.text:
The editor has these fields:

  • Name and Description.
  • Filter expression: the EL expression evaluated against each event. An empty expression matches every event.
  • Routing: the routing rules. Add start rule adds a create-workflow rule for the composition's workflow; Add dispatch rule adds a workflow-dispatch rule. Each rule has a remove button.

Below the form, the Matching events panel evaluates the current filter against the 200 most recent events and shows how many match (for example "12 of 200 recent events match"), how many events could not be evaluated together with the first error, and the matching events, each linking to its Event Stream page.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
On top of the usual subscription checks, the workbench reports:

Code Severity Meaning FOREIGN_WORKFLOW_ROUTE Error A create-workflow rule does not start this composition's workflow by name (it uses another name or a workflowDefinitionId). ENABLED_IGNORED Warning The draft sets enabled. Subscriptions are published disabled; enable them in the workbench after publishing. OVERLAPPING_SUBSCRIPTION Warning Another enabled published subscription, not part of this composition, already starts this composition's workflow.

docs.title: Publishing and enabling
docs.text:
A subscription needs the composition's workflow to be published already, or selected in the same publish.

Publishing never turns automation on by itself:

  • A new subscription (no published subscription with that name exists yet) is published disabled.
  • Republishing a subscription that this composition already published keeps its enabled state and its Process events from time.
  • If you rename a subscription item that was already published, publishing it creates a new subscription (disabled) and disables the previously published subscription. The old subscription is kept, not deleted; it is still listed on the Events → Subscriptions page, where you can delete it.
  • If a forced publish overwrites a same-name subscription that this composition did not publish, the subscription is left disabled (its Process events from time is kept).
  • Turning the subscription on or off (here or on the Events → Subscriptions page) does not count as a change outside the workbench.

Once a subscription is published, the editor header shows an Enabled switch. The switch is disabled (with the tooltip "Publish the workflow before enabling this subscription") until the composition's workflow is published. Enabling a subscription sets its Process events from time to now, so earlier events are ignored; only new events start or resume runs. Turning the switch off disables the subscription.

Removing a subscription draft, or deleting the composition, leaves the published subscription as it is (enabled or not). Disable or delete it on the Events → Subscriptions page.

docs.title: Workflows
docs.text:
Workflows let you define a multi-step automation — including branching, human approvals, timed waits, and event-triggered branches — as a versioned, visually authored graph of nodes. Every workflow run operates on a single subject (an issue, a pull request, a Jira ticket, or a named subject created by a schedule trigger) and drives that run's tasks.

If you haven't read Concepts yet, it introduces subjects, runs, events, and schedule triggers.

docs.title: Node Types
docs.text:
Node Type Purpose start Workflow entry point; declares the inputs the workflow expects (see Workflow Input Contract) end Workflow termination action Creates a task for an action type and waits for it to complete before advancing. This is the only way an action type is ever executed; every action type appears in the editor palette. human-task Pauses execution until a user completes a form through the Inbox (see Human-Task Nodes) wait Pauses the instance for a fixed duration, then resumes automatically receive-event Pauses the instance until a matching stream event is dispatched to it

The main configuration of each node type:

Node Type Configuration start inputs: the run's declared inputs, each with name, type, required and description; only the standard inputs subject and event may be declared, and both have type object end None. Ends the run, or the current branch of a parallel region action actionType (an action type name, or sdk:<function>); inputs: a map of input name to EL expression; optional outputs to rename or require task outputs. Task outputs are merged into the run context under their names human-task Optional title and description; inputs shown to the person; outputs: the form fields, whose answers are merged into the context wait duration: an ISO-8601 duration such as PT1H or P1D receive-event eventType (required); optional match conditions, outputs ({contextKey, expression}), correlationKey, lookback and timeout (see Dispatching Events to a Waiting Workflow)

docs.title: Edges
docs.text:
Edges connect nodes. Each edge may carry a priority, an EL condition, a default flag, and a label. Conditions let a node branch to different next steps based on the values already in the run's context (e.g. an action's output, or a human-task's submitted answers). The rules are:

  • A node with a single outgoing edge uses an unconditional edge that is not marked default.
  • A node with conditional edges (an exclusive choice) needs exactly one default edge, without a condition. It is the fallback when no condition matches. This includes a node with a single conditional edge.
  • Mark an edge as default only for such conditional choices. A node has at most one default edge.
  • Several unconditional, non-default edges leaving one node form a fork: the branches run in parallel. Do not mix fork edges with conditional or default edges. Parallel branches must re-join at a single node before they reach an end node.
  • Edges leaving the same node should have distinct priorities.
  • A receive-event node with a timeout needs exactly one timeout edge plus a normal outgoing edge.

docs.title: Expressions
docs.text:
Conditions, action input mappings, human-task titles and receive-event settings are Jakarta Expression Language (EL) expressions, written without ${}. They read context.<key> (the run context: inputs and merged node outputs) and, where an event is involved, event.<field>. Action inputs can only read context; use context.event for the triggering event. Examples:

  • context.needsInfo == true
  • context.priority eq 'high' and not empty context.assignee
  • 'Review ' += context.subject.ref (join text with +=)

EL has no fallback operator. a || b is a boolean OR and ?? is not valid syntax. To fall back to a default value, use empty: empty context.label ? 'triage' : context.label.

docs.title: Authoring a Workflow
docs.text:
Navigate to Components > Workflows and click Create Workflow Definition. New definitions are scaffolded with a Start node (declaring the standard inputs subject and event, both required) connected directly to an End node — extend the graph from there.

The Design tab holds the workflow editor (Apitomy Flow 3.0.2). It lets you add and connect nodes, configure each node's inputs and outputs, and edit conditional edges. An action node must map every required input of its action type, usually from the run context (context.subject.id, context.subject.name, context.subject.ref, context.subject.repository, context.event) or from outputs of earlier nodes; optional inputs may be left unmapped. See Inputs, Placeholders and Mappings. Click Save to store your changes as draft content on the definition; they are not usable by running instances until you publish.

To build a workflow together with its action types and tools, with an AI assistant at hand, click Open in workbench (available once your changes are saved). See Workflow Workbench.

docs.title: Publishing and Versions
docs.text:
Click Publish on the workflow detail page to validate the saved draft and create a new immutable version. Publish is disabled while there are unsaved changes or validation errors. Publishing fails with a description of the problem if:

  • The graph is structurally invalid (e.g. disconnected nodes, missing Start/End, or edges that break the rules in Edges)
  • The graph contains a node type Axiom doesn't support
  • The Start node declares an input other than the standard inputs subject and event, declares one with a different type, or gives one a default value (see the Workflow Input Contract)

Each publish creates a new version. The Versions tab lists every published version, lets you diff any two versions side by side, and shows which version is currently active (currentVersion). Existing runs continue to use the version they were started with — publishing a new version never changes the definition an in-flight run is executing. The Runs tab lists the runs of the definition.

docs.title: Triggering a Workflow
docs.text:
A workflow run can be started in these ways:

  • Manually from a stream event — on an event's detail page (Events > Event Stream, then click an event), click Run workflow… and pick any published workflow. Workflows used by subscriptions that matched the event are listed first, under Suggested. You may supply a title and labels. The run is started as a create-workflow rule would start it: on the subject found or created from the event's ref, with the event in its context as event. Manual runs get the label trigger:manual. REST: POST /api/v1/stream/events/{eventId}/runs.
  • From a subscription — a subscription routing rule of type create-workflow finds or creates a subject from the triggering event's ref, then starts the specified definition with its declared subject and event (the triggering event's envelope) inputs in its context.
  • From a schedule trigger — see Schedule Triggers below.
  • By re-running a failed run — see Re-running a Failed Run below.

docs.title: Run Title, Labels, and Inputs
docs.text:
A run can have a title of at most 500 characters. A run gets one when it is started with one (for example from the Title field of an event's Run workflow… dialog, or the REST API), or when the workflow sets it with the axiom_set_workflow_run_title SDK function (see Axiom SDK Functions); lists and headers name other runs by their subject and workflow. Runs also carry free-form key/value labels (runs started by a schedule trigger are labeled trigger: schedule). A run cannot be started with supplied inputs: its inputs are always resolved by Axiom (see below).

A run's context starts with exactly the standard inputs its Start node declares: subject (always available) and event (available only when the run was started from a stream event). A declared optional input that is not available is absent; a declared required input that is not available stops the run from being created with Cannot start workflow "<name>": required input(s) not available: <names>. New workflows declare both inputs as required, so a workflow run by a schedule trigger must remove event or make it optional; otherwise each firing records lastOutcome failed: Cannot start workflow "<name>": required input(s) not available: event, and a re-run returns HTTP 400 with the same message. See the Workflow Input Contract.

The run's recorded inputs (the Inputs entry on the run's Overview tab) are the resolved standard inputs, without event; the event is shown as the run's trigger instead.

Workflow runs have no outputs. The result of each step is available from the task output of the corresponding action node (and the submitted answers of each human-task node).

docs.title: Concurrency Rule
docs.text:
A subject can have at most one active run per workflow definition (running or waiting status). Sequential runs of the same definition on a subject are fine once the previous run finishes, and runs of different definitions may be active on the same subject at the same time.

A trigger that would violate the rule is handled as follows:

Trigger Behavior Manual (Run workflow…, Re-run) Rejected with HTTP 409 create-workflow routing rule Skipped (not queued); the skip is recorded in the routing outcome Schedule trigger Skipped (not queued); the trigger's last outcome is recorded as skipped

docs.title: Schedule Triggers
docs.text:
A workflow definition can have zero or more schedule triggers, managed on the Triggers tab of the workflow definition page (REST: /api/v1/workflow/definitions/{workflowDefinitionId}/triggers/schedules). Each trigger has:

Field Purpose Cron A 5-field Unix cron expression (minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week), evaluated in UTC Subject name Required; the fixed subject every run attaches to (at most 246 characters) Enabled Whether the trigger fires

The subject is created on the first firing (with ref schedule:<subject name>) and reused on every later firing, so run history accumulates on one subject. Each trigger also reports:

  • Next run (nextRunAt) — when the trigger fires next; empty while disabled
  • Last run (lastRunAt) — when the trigger last fired
  • Last outcome (lastOutcome) — started, skipped (the subject already had an active run of the definition), or failed: <reason>

Axiom checks for due triggers every axiom.workflow.schedule-poll-interval (default 30s). Firing assumes a single Axiom node; running multiple nodes against one database is not supported for schedule triggers.

docs.title: Re-running a Failed Run
docs.text: On a subject's Runs tab, each failed run has a Re-run button. After you confirm, Axiom starts a new run of the latest published version of the same workflow on the same subject. The new run keeps the original title and labels, and gets the extra label rerunOf:<original run id>. Its inputs are resolved again from the subject's current state; a run that was started from a stream event is re-run from that event, so the new run has the same context.event. The workflow's actions run again. Only failed runs can be re-run (REST: POST /api/v1/workflow/runs/{runId}/rerun; other statuses are rejected with HTTP 409).

docs.title: Dispatching Events to a Waiting Workflow
docs.text:
Independent of create-workflow, a subscription routing rule of type workflow-dispatch broadcasts matching events to every workflow run currently parked at a receive-event node — regardless of which subscription originally started that run. Matching considers the parked node's declared event type and EL condition. When the event carries a recognizable ref, delivery is scoped to waiting runs on the correlated subject (all of them, across definitions); uncorrelated events are offered to every parked receive-event node of a matching type.

A receive-event node can also declare:

  • correlationKey — {subscriptionKey, eventKey} EL expressions. The subscription key is evaluated against the run context when the node is reached and stored with the parked branch; only events whose evaluated event key is equal can match. match conditions still apply.
  • lookback — which already-stored events can satisfy the node when it is reached: run-start (default; events since the run started), none (only events that arrive later), or an ISO-8601 duration such as PT10M (never earlier than the run's start). Only events that matched the filter of a subscription with a workflow-dispatch rule are eligible, and an event never resumes the same run twice.
  • timeout — an ISO-8601 duration. If no matching event arrives in time, the run follows the node's timeout edge (isTimeout: true). Timeouts are checked every axiom.workflow.wait-poll-interval.

A human-task node's optional title EL expression (e.g. 'Review ' += context.subject.ref) becomes the task's subject in the Inbox; it falls back to the node name.

docs.title: Following a Run
docs.text:
Runs is Axiom's landing page (/runs). It lists every workflow run across all subjects with its status, title, subject, workflow and version, start time and duration. Filter chips narrow the list; see Runs. The same filters are available on GET /api/v1/workflow/runs as the status, definitionId, subjectId, and label query parameters (and triggerEventId for runs started from one event). Each run detail page has these tabs:

  • Diagram — the node graph with the run's progress; a node's menu opens its task's execution log
  • Overview — a form with the title (when the run has one), the subject and workflow (each linked to its page), the workflow version, status, start and end times, labels, inputs, the failure reason, a link to the trace, the triggering event (when started from an event), the events that resumed the run, and the tasks created by action or human-task nodes with their outputs and logs
  • Timeline — the nodes the run passed through, in order
  • Execution Trace — the run's trace, which records every node transition — see Tracing
  • Lineage — where the run came from and what it produced

A run's status is running, waiting, completed, failed, or cancelled. The subject detail page's Runs tab lists every run (active and past) on that subject.

A run parked at a human-task node surfaces its pending task in the Inbox; a run parked at a wait node resumes automatically once its resume time elapses; a run parked at a receive-event node resumes once a matching event is dispatched to it.

docs.title: Cancelling a Run
docs.text: Cancellation is per run: use Cancel run on the run detail page of a running or waiting run (REST: POST /api/v1/workflow/runs/{runId}/cancel). Cancelling marks the run cancelled, fails any in-progress task the run created, and removes any pending wait or event-subscription state associated with it. A cancelled run cannot be resumed. Other runs on the same subject are unaffected.

docs.title: Axiom SDK Functions
docs.text:
The Axiom SDK is a set of functions for reading and updating Axiom data. They are available in two ways:

  • SDK action nodes — every SDK function appears in the workflow editor palette (as SDK: …, stored as sdk:<function>) and runs directly, without an AI agent
  • subjectId and runId default to the node's own run, so they can usually be left unmapped
  • the node's outputs join the run context without being declared: context.success, context.output (a message) and the function's result fields (for example context.title)
  • a failed call (for example an over-long title) fails the node, and so the run
  • Agent tools — an action type or session template can allow mcp__axiom-sdk__<function> in its Allowed Tools, making the function available to the agent through the axiom-sdk MCP server

The authoritative list lives in core/src/main/resources/axiom-sdk-functions.json:

Function Purpose axiom_list_subjects List subjects, filtered by name, labels, or ref; each result includes its derived active flag axiom_get_subject Get a subject (subjectId) including metadata, ref, and active axiom_create_subject Create a subject axiom_update_subject Update a subject's name, body, or labels axiom_update_subject_body Replace a subject's Markdown body axiom_add_subject_label / axiom_remove_subject_label Add or remove a subject label axiom_get_subject_thread Read a subject's thread axiom_add_thread_entry Post a message to a subject's thread axiom_list_events List events related to a subject axiom_get_task_status Get the status and details of a task on a subject axiom_respond_to_task Submit a response to a task awaiting human input axiom_get_workflow_run Get a workflow run (runId, required): title, status, subject, definition and version, labels, inputs, current node. In an sdk: action node, runId is filled in automatically with the node's own run. axiom_set_workflow_run_title Set a workflow run's title (runId, title; a blank title clears it; at most 500 characters). In an sdk: action node, runId is filled in automatically, so a node with actionType sdk:axiom_set_workflow_run_title and input title (for example 'Checking ' += context.subject.name) titles its own run. axiom_list_subject_runs List workflow runs for a subject (subjectId, required; optional status), newest first, at most 50 axiom_fire_event Fire a new event into Axiom for processing by subscriptions and workflows axiom_get_activity_log Read the activity log, optionally filtered by subject axiom_list_tools / axiom_list_action_types / axiom_list_agents List configured tools, action types, and agents

There are no SDK functions for creating tasks directly, closing or reopening subjects, or reports — work is started only by workflow runs, and subjects have no lifecycle of their own.

docs.title: Workflows in Configuration Packs
docs.text:
Workflow definitions (including their published version history) are included in Configuration Packs export/import, and can be generated by the AI Assistant's Configuration Assistant. Workflows in an imported pack or applied by the assistant are validated and published; unchanged workflows are not re-published.

Subscriptions that start workflows (create-workflow routing rules) may reference the workflow by name with workflowDefinitionName instead of workflowDefinitionId. Axiom resolves the name to the workflow's id when the subscription is created, updated, imported, or applied, which lets a pack or assistant session create a workflow and the subscription that starts it together.
